# How to Use AI to Build a Better Pre-Call Question Sheet

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-pre-call-question-sheet
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-08T14:08:03.327Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A good pre-call question sheet helps a client arrive with useful context instead of making you spend the first part of the conversation collecting basics. Here’s a practical way to use AI to draft one, review it, and make it sound like you.

Use AI to draft a short, specific pre-call question sheet from your offer, your audience, and the purpose of the conversation. Then edit every question until it sounds like something you would actually ask. AI should help you think through the structure, not replace your judgment. A pre-call sheet is useful when a conversation could go in several directions. It gives the other person a chance to gather details, and it gives you a clearer starting point. That matters whether you are preparing for a coaching consultation, a real estate conversation, a lending call, or a project discussion. Start with the decision the call needs to support Before you ask AI for questions, write one sentence that describes the purpose of the call. For example: “I need to understand whether this person is ready for a three-month coaching engagement.” Or: “I need enough context to decide whether this property conversation is a fit for my services.” That sentence keeps the form from becoming a general biography. You are not trying to learn everything about a person. You are gathering the context needed for a useful conversation and a clear next step. Give AI these five pieces of context: What you offer and who it is for. What the call is meant to clarify. What information you need before making a recommendation. What information you do not need or should not request. The tone you want the person to feel when they complete the sheet. Do not paste private information that the person has not agreed to share. You can describe the type of client and the type of call without including identifying details. A prompt that gives AI enough direction A vague request such as “Write a client questionnaire” usually creates a list that could belong to any business. Give AI a role, a goal, and limits. Try this: Prompt: “Act as a thoughtful intake designer for my business. I help [audience] with [specific problem]. This pre-call sheet is for a [type of call], and the decision we need to support is [decision]. Draft 10 questions that help me understand the current situation, desired outcome, obstacles, timing, and fit. Use plain language. Avoid questions that feel invasive, repetitive, or like a sales trap. Mark the five questions that are essential if the person only has a few minutes.” That first draft is not the finished sheet. Read it and mark three categories: questions you want to keep, questions that need a rewrite, and questions that reveal something you do not actually need to know. Shape the questions around five useful areas 1. Current situation Begin with what is happening now. Ask the person to describe the situation in their own words. “What are you trying to solve right now?” is often more useful than asking them to choose from a long list of problems. A short answer can give you language to revisit during the call. 2. Desired outcome Ask what a meaningful improvement would look like. Keep the question concrete: “What would you like to be different after we work together?” This helps separate a broad wish from an outcome you can discuss responsibly. 3. Obstacles and past attempts Ask what has made the problem difficult and what they have already tried. This prevents you from repeating advice that did not fit. It also helps you understand whether the person wants information, a plan, accountability, or a different kind of support. 4. Timing and readiness Timing questions can be simple. Ask whether there is a date, event, deadline, or reason the conversation matters now. You can also ask what needs to be true before they take the next step. Do not pressure someone to provide an answer they do not have. 5. Call expectations End by asking what they want to leave the call with. They may want a recommendation, a few options, a rough plan, or a candid assessment of fit. Knowing that beforehand makes it easier to guide the conversation. Make the sheet easier to complete Once AI has grouped the questions, ask it to reduce repetition and place the questions in a natural order. Then make the sheet practical for a real person. Put the most useful questions first. Use one idea per question. Explain why a detailed answer helps when that is not obvious. Offer a “not sure yet” option when it makes sense. Keep optional questions separate from required ones. Ask for short answers unless a longer answer is genuinely helpful. Next, ask AI to create two versions: a five-question quick version and a longer version for people who want to share more. You can choose the right version based on the call type without rebuilding the process each time. Run a tone and usefulness review AI-generated forms can sound formal even when the underlying questions are good. Paste the draft back into AI with a sample of your own writing and ask for a tone review. Tell it to point out phrases that sound stiff, vague, judgmental, or overly promotional. You can ask for alternatives, but you should choose the final wording. Then do a human test. Read each question aloud. If you would never say it in a conversation, rewrite it. If two questions would produce the same answer, keep the clearer one. If a question makes you wonder what you would do with the answer, remove it or explain its purpose. Turn responses into a call plan The real value of the sheet comes after it is completed. Ask AI to organize the responses into a one-page preparation note with four sections: The person’s stated situation and desired outcome. Questions or details that need clarification. Topics to discuss during the call. A few possible next steps, clearly labeled as options rather than promises. Review that note yourself before the call. Correct anything AI misunderstood. Separate what the person actually said from your interpretation. This keeps the conversation grounded and makes it easier to listen instead of trying to construct the entire call in real time. After the call, you can use the same structure to record the agreed next action, the person’s open questions, and the date for follow-up. That creates a clean handoff from preparation to follow-through. For a related process, see how to turn a discovery call transcript into next actions . Keep improving the question sheet Do not change the sheet after every single call. Review it after several conversations and look for patterns. Which questions produce answers you use? Which ones are skipped? Where do people seem confused? Ask AI to summarize those patterns from anonymized notes, then decide what to change. Your question sheet should become shorter and clearer over time. It should help the right person arrive prepared, help you ask better follow-up questions, and help both of you agree on what happens next. That is a small workflow, but it can remove a surprising amount of scattered preparation from your week. If you want to build the larger system around content, follow-up, and business operations, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should a pre-call question sheet include?
A: It should ask about the person's current situation, desired outcome, obstacles, timing, and what they want from the conversation. Keep questions connected to the decision they are trying to make.

Q: Can AI write the questions without knowing my business?
A: AI can draft a starting point, but the quality depends on the context you provide. Give it your offer, audience, call goal, boundaries, and examples of questions you already ask.

Q: How many questions should I send before a call?
A: Use only the number you can review before the conversation. A short set of focused questions is usually more useful than a long form that feels like homework.

Q: Should every prospect receive the same question sheet?
A: Start with a core set, then adjust a few questions for the offer, audience, or kind of conversation. The sheet should feel relevant while still giving you consistent information.

Q: How do I keep AI-generated questions from sounding generic?
A: Add real language from your calls, remove questions you would not ask out loud, and ask AI to rewrite the sheet in your natural tone. Read the final version as if you were the person filling it out.

# How to Use AI to Write a Personal Referral Request

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-personal-referral-request
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-07T13:53:56.265Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A referral request works best when it feels personal, specific, and easy to answer. Here is a simple AI workflow for drafting one without handing over your relationships or your voice.

Yes, you can use AI to write a personal referral request, but you shouldn't ask it to invent the relationship. Give it the real context, the kind of person you help, and the specific introduction you would appreciate. Then edit the draft until it sounds like you. That distinction matters. A referral request is not a broadcast promotion. It's a small conversation with someone who already knows you, has seen some of your work, or has chosen to stay connected. AI can help you find the words, but the trust comes from the truth behind them. A simple AI workflow for a better referral request Start with one person, not a list. Open a note and write five plain-language answers: Who is this person to me? What do I appreciate about our relationship? What problem do I help solve? What kind of person might benefit from that help? What would a useful introduction look like? Don't polish your answers. The rough version is useful because it contains details a generic prompt won't. You might write that the person attended a workshop, introduced you to a colleague last year, or often talks with business owners who feel stuck with follow-up. Keep the information accurate and share only what the draft needs. Then ask AI to draft a message with a clear role. You could say: Prompt: “Act as an editing partner. Write a short referral request to someone I already know. Use the context below. Make it warm, specific, and easy to answer. Do not exaggerate, pressure the reader, or add facts I didn't provide. Include one natural question and keep the message conversational. Here is the context: [paste your five answers].” The request for an editing partner helps set the tone. You're asking for a draft, not handing over the relationship. Give the message a useful shape A good referral request usually has four parts. The parts don't need to appear as formal sections in the final message, but they give you something to check. 1. Reconnect with a real detail Begin with the reason you're reaching out. Mention a conversation, project, event, or shared interest that actually exists. “I was thinking about our conversation on client follow-up” is stronger than “I hope you're doing well” by itself. This detail does two jobs. It reminds the reader who you are in relation to each other, and it shows that the message wasn't copied to everyone in your contacts. If AI gives you a vague opening, replace it. 2. State the problem you solve Describe the problem in the words your audience might use. A coach might help a business owner turn scattered ideas into a repeatable content plan. A lender might help a buyer understand the next steps in a financing process. A consultant might help a team document work that currently lives in one person's head. Keep this part narrow. “I help businesses grow” gives the reader nothing useful to remember. A clear problem gives them a way to recognize a possible referral. 3. Describe the referral you want Ask for a situation, not a perfect lead profile. You can say, “If someone in your circle mentions that they have plenty of ideas but no consistent way to turn them into content, would you feel comfortable introducing us?” That request gives the person a listening cue. They don't have to search their entire network or guess what you mean by “anyone who needs help.” They only need to remember a conversation that fits. 4. Make the next step small One simple question is enough. You might ask whether anyone comes to mind, or whether the person would be comfortable forwarding a short introduction. Don't attach a long explanation to the first request. If they respond, you can provide the details they need. Use AI to improve the draft, not to make it sound bigger After AI gives you a first draft, run three editing passes. Truth pass: Check every claim, name, date, and relationship detail. Delete anything that wasn't in your notes. Voice pass: Read the message aloud. Replace words you don't normally use. Shorten sentences that feel formal or polished in the wrong way. Friction pass: Ask whether the reader knows what you're asking, why you're asking them, and what they should do next. If any answer is unclear, revise the message. You can ask AI to help with each pass. Try: “Point out any sentence that sounds generic, pressuring, or unsupported. Do not rewrite yet.” Then make the decisions yourself. A useful review should reveal weak spots without turning your message into a different person's voice. You can also ask for three versions with different levels of familiarity: one for a close contact, one for a past client, and one for a professional acquaintance. Use the version that matches the relationship. A past client may welcome a direct request, while a newer contact may need a little more context first. What to leave out of an AI referral workflow Don't paste an entire contact record into a writing prompt just because you can. A referral request rarely needs a person's private history, personal circumstances, or unrelated notes. Use the minimum context needed to draft a respectful message. Don't ask AI to create urgency you don't feel. A message that implies a deadline, scarcity, or special opportunity can damage a relationship when none of those things are real. Ask clearly, give the other person room to decline, and keep the tone steady. Don't send the same request to every person in your network. You can reuse the structure, but the opening, problem, and request should fit the individual. Personalization isn't adding a first name to a template. It's showing why this person is a sensible person to ask. Turn one request into a repeatable habit If you want referrals to become part of your normal business rhythm, create a small record after each conversation. Note who you contacted, why the relationship made sense, what you asked for, and whether you need to follow up. AI can turn those notes into a simple reminder list or help you draft a respectful follow-up later. Keep the follow-up connected to the original request. You might say, “I wanted to follow up on my note from last week. No pressure at all. I was curious whether anyone came to mind who is trying to solve that problem.” If the person says no, thank them and leave the relationship in good shape. You can also use the same workflow after delivering a useful result, completing a project, or reconnecting with a past client. The timing should make sense in the relationship. A request is easier to receive when it follows a real conversation rather than appearing without context. Your next step Choose one person who already knows your work. Write the five rough answers, ask AI for a short draft, and edit it in your own voice. Before you send it, make sure the request names one problem, one kind of introduction, and one easy next step. That is enough to begin. You don't need a complicated campaign. You need a truthful message, a clear reason for reaching out, and the discipline to treat the response as a conversation instead of a transaction. If you want a larger system for turning AI into consistent content, follow-up, and business support, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI write a referral request for me?
A: Yes. AI can help organize your context and draft a message, but you should review every sentence before sending it. The final request should reflect your real relationship and a genuine reason to reach out.

Q: What information should I give AI first?
A: Give it the relationship, the person's likely need, the help you provide, the kind of introduction you would value, and the tone you want. Leave out private information that isn't needed.

Q: How long should a referral request be?
A: Keep the first message short enough to read quickly. A few clear paragraphs are usually enough to reconnect, explain who you can help, and make one simple request.

Q: Should I send the AI draft exactly as written?
A: No. Treat the draft as a starting point. Replace generic wording, add a real detail from your relationship, and remove anything that doesn't sound like something you would say.

Q: What if I don't know exactly who to ask for?
A: Ask for a situation instead of a job title. For example, you might describe the kind of problem someone is facing and invite the person to think of anyone who has mentioned it recently.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Workshop Into a Content Brief

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-workshop-content-brief
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-06T14:24:28.915Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A workshop can contain weeks of useful ideas, but only if you give those ideas a structure before you start writing. This practical workflow shows you how to use AI to sort the material into a focused content brief, check the message, and choose the next pieces to create.

Yes, you can use AI to turn a workshop into a content brief, but the useful result comes from giving the tool a clear job. Ask it to identify the audience's problem, organize the strongest teaching points, separate examples from claims, and recommend a small set of content pieces. Then you review the brief before anything is published. This matters because a workshop usually has more material than one article can hold. If you ask AI to simply summarize the recording, you may get a long recap with no clear message. A content brief gives the material a destination. It helps you decide what to say, who needs to hear it, and what the reader should do next. Start with the business outcome Before you paste in notes or a transcript, write one sentence that explains why you want to reuse the workshop. Keep it specific. For example: I want to help independent agents understand how to answer common seller questions, then invite them to request a planning conversation. The sentence does two jobs. It tells AI what to look for, and it gives you a test for every recommendation. If a proposed topic does not support the audience or the conversation you want to start, it probably does not belong in this brief. Choose one primary audience as well. Small business owners is broad. A solo consultant who has useful expertise but posts inconsistently gives the writing a real person to serve. You can create another brief for another audience later. Give AI clean source material Use the best material you already have: a transcript, workshop outline, speaker notes, chat questions, or your own follow-up notes. You do not need to make the source perfect first. You do need to label each item so the tool can tell the difference between what you taught, what an attendee asked, and what you want to add later. Remove information that should not appear in public content. That may include private contact details, confidential business information, or a participant's personal situation. A brief can be accurate without repeating sensitive details. If you have a transcript, ask AI to preserve the meaning while cleaning filler words and repeated points. If you only have an outline, tell it that the source is incomplete. That small instruction helps you spot places where a draft needs your judgment rather than invented detail. A useful first prompt You can begin with a prompt like this: You are helping me plan content for [audience]. The business goal is [goal]. Review the workshop material below. First, list the audience's main problem in one sentence. Then group the teaching into three to five themes. For each theme, show the practical lesson, the supporting example from the source, and any statement that needs my review. Do not add facts that are not in the source. End with three possible content angles. That prompt asks for sorting and judgment support. It does not ask AI to make up a story, add a statistic, or present an unverified promise. Shape the raw material into a brief Once AI has grouped the workshop, ask it to format the result into a brief with these sections: Audience: Who is this for, and what are they trying to solve? Working title: A clear question or promise, not a vague topic. Core message: The one idea the reader should remember. Three to five teaching points: The smallest useful sequence for understanding the idea. Source examples: Examples from the workshop that make the teaching concrete. Review notes: Claims, numbers, names, or recommendations you must check. Call to action: The next reasonable step for this audience. Content formats: The primary piece and two or three smaller follow-ups. The core message is the most important section. If you cannot say it in one or two sentences, the workshop may contain several separate articles. Split them. One focused article is easier to write, easier to read, and easier for a potential client to remember. Choose one primary piece Do not begin by asking for ten social posts. Choose the piece that deserves the deepest thought. That might be an article answering the audience's main question, an email that teaches one decision, or a short guide that helps someone take the next step. Then ask AI to create a simple outline for that piece from the approved brief. Give it boundaries such as the intended reader, approximate length, required sections, and tone. Tell it which examples are approved and which points still need review. After the primary piece is finished, reuse its approved ideas for shorter content. This is where a workshop becomes a system rather than a one-time writing task. One lesson can become a useful article, a short email, several conversation prompts, and a follow-up question for your audience. For a related approach, see AI content repurposing from one video . The same principle applies here: approve the central message before adapting it into smaller formats. Use human review where it counts AI is helpful at sorting, labeling, and suggesting structure. You remain responsible for the meaning. Read the brief and ask four questions: Does this describe a problem my audience actually recognizes? Would I say the core message this plainly in a real conversation? Are the examples faithful to the workshop? Does the next step fit the reader's level of interest? Pay close attention to confident wording. A draft can make an ordinary suggestion sound like a guarantee. Replace promises with clear guidance. If a point depends on a current rule, product detail, price, statistic, or outside claim, mark it for verification or leave it out. Your own language also matters. Add the phrases you use with clients, the questions people ask before they buy, and the distinctions you make that others skip. Those details are what turn a generic summary into content with a point of view. Turn the brief into a repeatable weekly habit At the end of each workshop, save four things in one folder: the source material, the cleaned transcript or notes, the approved brief, and the final content. The next time you teach the topic, you can update the brief instead of starting from a blank page. You can also maintain a short list of audience questions that the workshop did not answer. Feed those questions into your next planning session. The article How to turn client questions into better content can help you build that list from real conversations. Keep the workflow simple: collect, sort, review, create, and reuse. The goal is not to produce the largest number of posts. The goal is to make your best teaching easier for the right person to find and act on. What a strong brief gives you A strong brief gives you a clean starting point, a clear audience, and a message that can survive across formats. It also shows you where your source material is thin. That is valuable. You can return to the workshop, add your own example, or remove a point that is not ready to publish. When your workshop has a clear offer behind it, connect the content to that offer without forcing the sale. A focused offer document can help you make that connection; see how to create a clear one-page offer brief with AI . Start with your next workshop or training. Give AI the audience, the business goal, and the source material. Ask for themes, examples, review notes, and a few content angles. Then make the final call yourself. That is how you turn teaching you have already done into content that keeps working for your business.

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking for a content brief?
A: Give it the workshop transcript, outline, notes, or a combination of those materials. Also include the audience, the business goal, and any points that must remain accurate.

Q: Can AI create the whole content plan from one workshop?
A: It can suggest a plan, but you should choose the final topics. Review the suggestions for accuracy, audience fit, and whether each piece supports a real business conversation.

Q: How long should a content brief be?
A: Keep it short enough to use. A few focused sections covering the audience, promise, key points, proof, call to action, and formats are usually enough for a first draft.

Q: How do I keep the content from sounding generic?
A: Give AI examples of your real language, specific audience questions, and clear points of view. Then edit the draft so it sounds like a person with an opinion, not a summary tool.

Q: What should I do after the brief is approved?
A: Create one primary piece first, such as an article or email. Use the approved message to guide shorter posts, a follow-up email, or a conversation prompt.

# How to Use AI to Create a Clear One-Page Offer Brief

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-one-page-offer-brief
Pillar: The Authority Agent Operating System™
Published: 2026-08-05T13:52:37.495Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A one-page offer brief gives you a clear reference point for sales conversations, content, and follow-up. Here is a practical way to use AI to build one from what you already know about your business.

Use AI to create a one-page offer brief by giving it your real business notes, asking it to organize the offer into a fixed set of sections, and then editing every claim until the page sounds like you. The goal is not to have AI invent a clever slogan. The goal is to make your offer easier to explain, sell, and turn into useful content. If your offer lives in scattered notes, old sales emails, voice memos, and your own head, every conversation starts from scratch. A short brief gives you a dependable reference point. It can guide a discovery call, a landing page, a follow-up email, or a post that answers a question your audience is already asking. What belongs in a one-page offer brief? Keep the document practical. A reader should understand the offer without needing a long background story. Start with these sections: Best-fit person: Describe who the offer is for and what situation they are in now. Problem: State the costly, frustrating, or time-consuming problem the person wants to address. Desired outcome: Describe the change your service is designed to help create. Keep the wording specific without promising a result you cannot control. Method: Summarize the main steps, conversations, deliverables, or decisions included in the work. Boundaries: Say what the offer does not include. Clear boundaries prevent the page from becoming a list of everything you could possibly do. Proof: Add only evidence you are permitted to use, such as your own relevant experience, a process explanation, or an approved example. Next step: Tell the right person what to do next, such as booking a call, completing an application, or sending a question. This structure works for a coach, consultant, real estate agent, lender, or creator because it connects the offer to a real business conversation. It also gives AI enough shape to help without handing over your judgment. Gather source material before you prompt AI can arrange information, but it cannot know the details of your service unless you provide them. Collect the material you already have. You might include your current website copy, a service description, a list of deliverables, questions prospects ask, notes from recent calls, and a short explanation of who should not buy the offer. Do not paste private information that the brief does not need. Remove names, contact details, financial records, and anything confidential. A useful source packet can be general and still be concrete. For example, instead of sharing a client identity, write, “The buyer had many inquiries but no consistent follow-up process.” Also separate facts from hopes. “I send a weekly review and provide three planning calls” is a description of your process. “Every client doubles revenue” is a result claim that would need support. Leave unsupported claims out. Use a prompt that asks for structure Ask AI to act as an editor and organizer, not as the owner of your business. You can start with a prompt like this: “Create a one-page offer brief from the source material below. Use these headings: Best-fit person, problem, desired outcome, method, boundaries, proof, and next step. Keep the language plain and specific. Do not invent facts, results, testimonials, credentials, or features. Mark any missing information with [NEEDS MY INPUT]. Give me a draft and then a short list of claims I should verify.” Paste your source material below the prompt. If you use Claude, you can place the approved source material and writing preferences in a Project, then ask for a fresh draft when the offer changes. The important part is the instruction: AI should work from your material and identify gaps instead of filling them with guesses. Edit the draft in three passes The first draft is a sorting exercise. Your editing is what makes the brief useful. Check accuracy. Read each sentence and ask whether it describes what you actually do. Remove invented details, broad promises, and language that makes the service sound larger than it is. Check clarity. Replace abstract words with observable actions. “Improve your business” is vague. “Create a weekly follow-up routine for new inquiries” gives the reader something they can picture. Check fit. Read the page as one specific person. Would they recognize their current problem? Would they understand whether the offer is for them? Would the next step feel clear? Read the page out loud. If you would never say a sentence in a real conversation, rewrite it. Your brief should sound like a strong explanation you could give on a call, not like a brochure assembled from general business language. Turn one brief into daily business assets Once the brief is approved, keep it as a source document. Ask AI to create related assets while preserving the same audience, promise, boundaries, and next step. You can request a discovery-call opening, five educational posts, a short FAQ email, a follow-up message, or a page of objections and responses. Review each asset against the brief. This prevents a common problem: your website says one thing, your sales conversation says another, and your follow-up introduces a third version of the offer. Consistent language makes it easier for a potential client to understand what you do and decide whether to continue. You can also feed recurring questions back into the brief. If people repeatedly ask whether the service includes a certain task, add that answer to the boundaries or method section. If prospects use a phrase that describes the problem better than your original wording, consider adding their plain-language phrase to the document. Keep the brief alive, but keep it short A one-page brief is not meant to become your entire operations manual. It is a decision tool. It should help you answer four questions quickly: Who is this for? What problem does it address? How do I help? What should the right person do next? Store the approved version where you can find it, and name it clearly. When you change the offer, update the brief before asking AI to create new sales or content materials. That small habit gives every new draft a better starting point. AI is most useful here when it reduces the friction between what you know and what you need to communicate. You supply the experience, boundaries, and judgment. AI helps you sort the material into a clear working document. That is enough to make your next conversation, email, and piece of content more focused. If you want a broader system for turning your expertise into repeatable business workflows, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What is an AI offer brief?
A: It is a short working document that explains who your offer serves, the problem it addresses, the outcome you provide, what the process includes, and what a qualified person should do next. AI helps organize your raw material, but you approve the final message.

Q: What should I give AI before asking it to write the brief?
A: Give it your current offer description, notes from real conversations, common questions, deliverables, boundaries, and any proof you are allowed to share. Specific source material produces a more useful first draft.

Q: Should my offer brief include pricing?
A: Only if pricing is already part of your public sales process. If the price depends on scope, leave it out and explain how someone can ask for the right next step.

Q: Can I use one offer brief for every audience?
A: Use one core brief as your source of truth, then create audience-specific versions when the problem, language, or buying context changes. Keep the underlying promise consistent.

Q: How often should I revise the brief?
A: Review it when your offer changes or when repeated conversations reveal confusion. You do not need to rewrite it on a schedule if the message still matches the work you deliver.

# How to Use AI to Build a 30-Day Prospect Follow-Up Plan

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-30-day-prospect-follow-up-plan
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-04T14:07:12.410Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A good follow-up plan should help a prospect make a decision, not pressure them into one. Here is a simple way to use AI to organize the conversation, find useful next steps, and create a month of personal follow-up.

Yes, you can use AI to build a 30-day prospect follow-up plan from one conversation. The useful version starts with your actual notes, separates what the prospect said from what you assume, and turns their questions into a small sequence of helpful messages. You still review and send each message yourself. The goal is not to fill a calendar with reminders. The goal is to remember the person's situation well enough to follow up with something relevant. Start with the conversation, not a generic template Before you ask AI to write anything, gather the notes you already have. These might come from a discovery call, a voice memo after a meeting, an email exchange, or a few handwritten points. You do not need polished notes. You need the raw material. Pull out five things: The result the prospect wants. The problem or frustration they described. The questions they asked. The concern that may slow down a decision. The next step, timing, or permission you discussed. Be careful with the difference between a fact and an interpretation. “They said they need to review the budget” is a fact from your conversation. “They are probably worried about price” is an interpretation. Ask AI to label those separately so your follow-up does not treat a guess as something the prospect told you. Use one clear prompt to create the plan Give AI a job, a source, and boundaries. You could start with a prompt like this: “Act as my follow-up planning assistant. Use the conversation notes below to create a 30-day nurture plan for one prospect. Separate confirmed details from assumptions. Suggest five or fewer touches. For each touch, include the purpose, a useful topic, the best format, and a short draft. Do not invent facts, promises, deadlines, testimonials, or resources. Keep the language warm, direct, and low-pressure. Every touch must connect to something the prospect said or asked.” Then paste your notes. If the notes include sensitive information, remove anything AI does not need to complete the task. The more specific your source material is, the less likely the drafts are to sound like messages copied from a marketing sequence. Ask for a plan before you ask for finished copy. This gives you a chance to reject a weak idea early. If AI suggests three versions of “just checking in,” the problem is not the wording. The problem is that the follow-up has no purpose. Give every touch a reason to exist A practical 30-day plan might include a small number of moments such as these: After the conversation: Send a concise recap of what you heard, the agreed next step, and one question if something remains unclear. When you can answer a question: Share a short explanation, example, checklist, or process that helps with the issue the prospect raised. When a concern needs room: Acknowledge the concern without trying to talk the person out of it. Invite them to tell you what information would help. Near the timing you discussed: Refer back to the timing in your notes and ask whether the situation has changed. At the end of the period: Offer a clear next step, or make it easy for the prospect to say that now is not the right time. These are categories, not a rule that every prospect needs five messages. Some people need two thoughtful follow-ups. Others need more time and a useful resource between conversations. The plan should reflect the relationship and the prospect's stated pace. Turn the plan into messages that sound like you AI often produces language that is tidy but lifeless. Your notes can fix that if you add a short voice guide. Tell AI whether you write in short paragraphs, whether you prefer a conversational opening, which words you never use, and how direct your calls to action should be. You can also paste a few examples of your own writing and ask for a draft that follows those patterns without copying any sentence. Then edit the draft with three questions: Would I say this out loud to the person? Does this message prove that I remember their situation? Is there a useful reason to respond, even if they are not ready to buy? Delete flattery that you do not mean. Delete urgency you cannot support. Delete broad claims about what everyone needs. A personal follow-up is often shorter after editing. Build a review step into the workflow Do not let the plan disappear into a document. Put each touch into the place where you manage follow-up, then add a review step before sending. Your review can be as simple as checking four fields: source note, intended date, purpose, and draft. Before a message goes out, confirm that the timing still makes sense. Check names, numbers, links, and any details about your service. Make sure the message does not promise an outcome you cannot promise. If the prospect has already answered the question, do not send a message that repeats it. This human check is also where you decide whether the right next action is a message, a call, a useful introduction, or no contact for a while. AI can help you see the options. It should not decide what respect looks like in your relationship. Measure the quality of the conversation You do not need a complicated report. After each touch, record what happened in plain language. Did the prospect reply? Did they ask a better question? Did they clarify their timing? Did they say no? A clear no is useful information too, because it keeps you from treating silence as a permanent invitation. At the end of 30 days, ask AI to summarize the thread and suggest one of three actions: continue with a specific reason, schedule a future check-in the prospect agreed to, or close the loop respectfully. Include the original notes and your follow-up record so the suggestion is grounded in the actual exchange. You can reuse the same workflow for a coach reviewing an enrollment conversation, a consultant waiting on a proposal decision, a lender helping a borrower understand next steps, or an agent staying connected with a future client. The structure stays consistent. The source conversation and the useful answer change. The simple standard for better follow-up A good AI-assisted follow-up plan should help you remember, respond, and make the next step clear. It should not make you sound busier, louder, or more automated. Start with one conversation this week. Ask AI to identify what the person actually needs, draft a short plan, and point out every assumption. Then revise the plan until each touch earns its place. When the workflow is built around listening, AI gives you more consistency without taking the relationship out of your hands. If you want a larger system for turning your knowledge and follow-up into a repeatable business process, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking for a follow-up plan?
A: Give it your notes from the conversation, the prospect's stated goal, concerns, timing, and the next step you discussed. Remove private details that are not needed for the writing task.

Q: How often should I contact a prospect during 30 days?
A: Choose a rhythm you can maintain and that fits the conversation. A few useful, spaced-out touches are usually better than sending a message every day.

Q: Should AI send the follow-up messages automatically?
A: Keep a human review step. AI can organize ideas and draft language, but you should check the timing, facts, tone, and whether each message gives the prospect a real reason to hear from you.

Q: What if I do not have enough information for 30 days of content?
A: Do not fill the calendar with generic messages. Ask AI to create fewer touches, suggest one useful resource, and identify the question you should answer next.

# How to Use AI to Turn Meeting Notes Into a Decision Log

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-meeting-notes-decision-log
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-03T14:03:14.597Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Meeting notes are only useful when they help you remember what was decided and what happens next. This practical AI workflow turns rough notes into a decision log your business can actually use.

Use AI to turn meeting notes into a decision log by giving it the raw notes, asking it to separate decisions from discussion, and requiring it to label every action with an owner, deadline, and next check-in. Then review the result yourself before it becomes the official record. This matters because a meeting can feel productive while still leaving everyone with a different understanding of what happens next. A decision log gives you one place to see what was chosen, why it was chosen, who is responsible, and what still needs an answer. What a useful decision log contains A decision log is not a transcript. It is a short operating record. Each entry should help someone understand the decision without rereading an hour of conversation. Date and topic: Identify when the discussion happened and what business issue it covered. Decision: State the choice in one clear sentence. Reason: Capture the main factors that led to the choice. Owner: Name the person responsible for the next action. Due date: Include a specific date when one exists. Open questions: List anything that could change the decision. Next review: Record when the team will check progress or revisit the choice. That structure keeps the record useful for a solo business owner as well as a small team. You are creating a memory for the business, not just a summary for the people who attended. The five-step AI workflow 1. Gather the real notes Start with the notes you actually have. They may come from a notebook, a voice memo, a meeting transcript, or a rough document with incomplete sentences. Do not spend an hour rewriting them first. The roughness is exactly what the workflow is meant to handle. Before sharing them, remove information that should not be entered into your chosen AI tool. That can include passwords, payment details, private health information, or sensitive personal information. If a detail is not needed to understand the decision, leave it out. 2. Give AI the business context AI produces a better working draft when it knows the purpose of the meeting. Tell it what kind of business you run, what outcome the meeting was meant to produce, and who the audience for the final log will be. For example, you might write: “I run a consulting business. These are rough notes from a planning meeting about a new service. Create a decision log for me and my assistant. Keep decisions separate from ideas, and do not assume a detail that is not in the notes.” That last instruction is essential. It tells the tool to organize the information without pretending that missing information is settled. 3. Ask for separation, not a polished summary A broad request such as “summarize this meeting” may produce a readable paragraph, but it can blur the difference between a suggestion and a final choice. Ask for distinct sections instead. Use a prompt like this: “Review the notes below. Return four sections: decisions made, action items, unresolved questions, and ideas that were discussed but not approved. For every action item, include the owner and deadline only when stated. If the notes are unclear, write ‘needs confirmation.’ Do not invent names, dates, reasons, or commitments.” This format gives you a first pass that is easy to inspect. It also creates a useful boundary around what AI is allowed to infer. In a business record, a visible gap is safer than a confident guess. 4. Turn the draft into a repeatable record Once the sections look accurate, ask AI to place them into a consistent template. Keep the template simple enough that you will use it every time. Ask for columns or headings such as decision, reason, owner, due date, status, and next review. If your business has several types of meetings, create a slightly different version for sales, operations, content, or client work. The basic fields can stay the same while the questions change. For a client meeting, you might add “client preference” and “client approval needed.” For a content meeting, you might add “audience problem” and “publication channel.” The record should reflect the work, not force every conversation into an identical shape. 5. Review and assign the next move Read the draft against the original notes. Check names, dates, decisions, and wording that could be interpreted more than one way. Correct anything that is wrong or too certain. Then choose one next move. Save the approved log where you keep business records, send a short follow-up message, or add the action items to your task system. AI has helped prepare the record, but the system becomes valuable only when a human uses it to move work ahead. How to keep the log accurate The most common problem is allowing a polished output to feel more reliable than the source notes. Set a few rules that protect the record. Ask AI to mark uncertain information instead of filling it in. Keep decisions and proposals in separate sections. Use exact dates when a deadline was stated. Do not assign an owner unless the meeting notes support that assignment. Have the decision maker approve the final wording when the choice affects a client, contract, budget, or team responsibility. You can also ask AI to run a quality check after it creates the log: “List every statement in this decision log that is not directly supported by the notes.” Review that list before you share the document. It gives you a second way to catch accidental assumptions. When this workflow is most useful Use it after meetings where choices get buried inside conversation. That may include deciding which offer to promote, setting a content theme, reviewing a lead process, planning a client project, or assigning work for the week. It is especially helpful when you are the person carrying most of the business in your head. A written record reduces the need to remember every detail and makes it easier to return to the reasoning behind a choice. It can also show you which decisions keep reopening because a question, owner, or deadline was never recorded. This workflow is not a substitute for judgment. It is a way to make your judgment easier to see and easier to act on. Start with one recurring meeting, use the same prompt for a few weeks, and adjust the template when you notice a missing field. Make meeting memory part of your operating system Your business does not need more notes. It needs notes that lead somewhere. When every important meeting produces a short decision log, you can review the past, see current commitments, and prepare the next conversation without starting from zero. That is a small AI workflow, but it solves a real business problem: good conversations disappearing before the work is finished. Build the habit around one meeting this week, then connect the approved actions to the rest of your follow-up process. Learn the AI System to build practical workflows that help your business create, follow up, and keep moving with fewer manual steps.

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI before asking it to organize meeting notes?
A: Give it the raw notes, the meeting purpose, the names or roles of people involved, and any known deadlines. Remove confidential details that do not belong in the tool you are using.

Q: Can AI decide what my business should do?
A: AI can sort, summarize, compare, and surface open questions. You should make the decision and review the final record before sharing it.

Q: How often should I update a decision log?
A: Update it after each meaningful meeting or decision. A short, consistent update is more useful than waiting until several weeks of notes have piled up.

Q: What if the meeting notes are incomplete?
A: Ask AI to mark uncertain details and create a list of questions to confirm. Do not let it fill gaps with guesses.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Voice Note Into a Client Update

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-voice-note-client-update
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-08-02T14:08:55.722Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A rough voice note can become a useful client update in minutes when you give AI the right job and review the result yourself. This workflow helps you capture the facts, choose the next step, and send a message that still sounds like you.

Yes, you can use AI to turn a rough voice note into a clear client update. The best workflow is to record the situation in your natural words, ask AI to sort the information, and then review a short draft before it leaves your hands. AI handles the organization. You handle the judgment, relationship, and final approval. This is useful when you are between appointments, leaving a property, finishing a coaching session, or thinking through a project while the details are still fresh. You do not need to stop and write a polished email before you have captured what happened. The simple voice-note-to-update workflow Use four stages: capture, sort, draft, and review. Keeping those stages separate makes the process easier to repeat and gives you a clear place to catch mistakes. 1. Capture the situation out loud Open your phone's voice recorder or the tool you already use for notes. Speak as if you are explaining the situation to a capable team member. Do not try to sound polished. Cover these five points: Who needs the update. What happened or changed. What you already did. What needs to happen next. What question, choice, or deadline belongs to the client. For example, you might say: “Send Jordan an update on the proposal. I reviewed the scope this morning. The timeline is still possible if we receive the photos by Thursday. I need Jordan to confirm whether the second review is included. Keep the message warm and short.” Notice that this is not a finished email. It is a private working note with the details AI needs to arrange. 2. Ask AI to separate facts from decisions Paste the transcript or a typed version of your note into your AI workspace. Start with an organizing prompt instead of asking for a perfect email immediately: “Read this voice note and separate it into four sections: confirmed facts, actions already taken, open questions, and next actions. Do not add information. Mark anything that is unclear.” This step matters because a voice note often blends what you know with what you think might happen. The sorting pass makes that difference visible. If AI marks something as unclear, answer the question yourself or remove the detail. 3. Turn the organized note into a client update After checking the organized version, ask for the message. Give it a clear job and a limit: “Using only the confirmed facts and approved next actions below, draft a client update. Begin with a friendly sentence. State what changed, what I have completed, and the next step. Put any question for the client in a separate sentence. Keep it under 150 words. Do not make promises that are not stated in the notes.” A good client update usually answers three questions: What do I need to know? What happens next? Do you need anything from me? If the draft does not answer those questions, revise the instructions instead of accepting a longer message. 4. Review before you send Read the draft as the client would read it. Check every name, date, amount, deadline, and promise. Make sure the message says what you mean, not merely what your voice note happened to imply. Then ask yourself: Is the main point visible in the first two sentences? Does the client know what happens next? Is there one clear request, if a request is needed? Did the draft add a fact I did not provide? Does it sound like something I would actually send? Make the final edits yourself. A client update is part of the relationship, so your judgment belongs in the last step. A prompt you can reuse Save this prompt in your notes: “You are helping me prepare a client update. First, separate my note into confirmed facts, completed actions, open questions, and next actions. Do not invent details. Then draft a concise message using only the confirmed information. Keep the tone warm, direct, and natural. Explain what changed, what happens next, and what the client needs to do, if anything. Flag uncertain details before drafting. I will review the message before sending it.” Attach your voice note transcript below the prompt. If the message is for a sensitive situation, add more direction about the tone, such as calm, reassuring, firm, or brief. How to make the workflow sound like you AI tends to produce language that is smooth but generic when it has no example of your communication style. Give it a small set of approved examples, then describe what you want to preserve. You might write: “Use short paragraphs. Start with the useful point. Be warm without excessive enthusiasm. Do not use sales language. Keep my direct phrasing.” The specific guidance is more useful than asking for a message that sounds human. You can also ask AI to show two versions: one that is very brief and one that includes a little more context. Choose the version that fits the relationship and the situation. More words do not automatically create more clarity. Where this workflow helps most This process works well for routine updates that still require your personal judgment. You could use it after a discovery call, during a project, after reviewing a document, or when a client is waiting for a decision from you. It also creates a useful record of your thinking. Once the update is sent, you can keep the organized note with the project materials. Later, that note can help you prepare the next conversation or document a repeated process. For a related workflow, see how to turn a discovery call transcript into next actions . If the communication involves confidential information, follow your existing privacy and record-keeping rules. Remove details that the AI tool does not need. You can ask for structure without sharing every sensitive fact. What not to delegate Do not ask AI to decide what you owe a client, whether a promise is realistic, or how to handle a serious conflict without your review. Those are business decisions, not formatting tasks. AI can help you see the message more clearly. It can point out a missing deadline or an unanswered question. It can give you a cleaner first draft. You are still the person who knows the history, the expectations, and the right next move. That distinction keeps the workflow practical. You are not handing over the relationship. You are removing the blank-page problem between a thought and a useful update. Start with one update today Choose one client who is waiting for information. Record a one-minute note using the five points above. Ask AI to sort it, draft it, and flag anything unclear. Review the message, send it, and save the prompt if the process helped. After a few repetitions, you will have a small communication system that fits the way you already work. That is where AI becomes useful in a real business: not as a replacement for your voice, but as support for the steps that make your voice easier to use consistently. If you want a broader system for using AI across content, follow-up, and daily operations, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI write a client update from a short voice note?
A: Yes. A short note can give AI enough raw material to organize the situation, draft a message, and list any missing details. You still need to check the facts and decide what should be sent.

Q: What should I include in a voice note for AI?
A: Include who the update is for, what changed, what has already happened, what happens next, and any deadline or question the client needs to answer.

Q: How do I keep the update in my voice?
A: Give AI a few examples of messages you like and describe the tone in plain language. Ask it to keep your natural level of warmth and brevity, then edit the draft before sending it.

Q: Should I send the AI draft without reviewing it?
A: No. Review names, dates, amounts, commitments, and tone. AI can organize your thoughts, but you remain responsible for the final communication.

Q: What if my voice note is disorganized?
A: That is fine. Tell AI to separate facts, decisions, open questions, and next actions before it writes the client-facing message.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Finished Project Into a Case Study

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-finished-project-case-study
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-08-01T14:02:31.201Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A finished project contains the raw material for a useful case study, but the story is often scattered across notes, emails, and memory. This workflow helps you organize what happened, show how you think, and create a draft you can review before sharing.

Yes, you can use AI to turn a finished project into a case study, but the best workflow starts with organization, not a blank-page writing prompt. Give the tool a clear record of the problem, your process, the work completed, and the facts you are allowed to share. Then ask it to arrange that material into a story, flag gaps, and wait for your review before anything is published. This matters because a case study is more than a compliment or a list of deliverables. It shows a prospective client how you think when a real problem lands on your desk. A useful case study can answer the questions a buyer is already carrying: What was difficult? What did you do first? What decisions did you make? What changed? What should someone like me expect from your process? Start with a fact file, not a polished story After a project ends, collect the source material in one document. You do not need to make it elegant. A rough fact file is often more useful because it preserves the details that disappear when you try to sound polished too early. Include sections such as: Starting point: What situation, question, or obstacle began the project? Desired outcome: What did the client or customer want to accomplish? Constraints: What limited the available time, budget, information, or options? Your actions: What did you do, in the order that matters? Key decisions: Which choices required judgment? Deliverables: What did you actually provide? Evidence: Which results, feedback, or observations are documented and approved? Lessons: What would you repeat or handle differently next time? Paste in your own notes, meeting summaries, project milestones, and approved feedback. Do not add details simply because they would make the story more dramatic. If the project involved a private person or business, remove identifying information until you know what can be shared. Give the AI a job with clear boundaries Your prompt should explain the role you want the tool to play and the limits it must follow. A short instruction such as “write a case study” leaves too many decisions open. The output may sound smooth while quietly filling gaps with assumptions. Try a prompt like this: “Act as an editorial assistant. Use only the information in the fact file below. Draft a case study for a prospective client who wants to understand our process. Organize it under Starting Point, Approach, Key Decisions, Work Completed, Outcome, and Lessons Learned. Do not invent numbers, quotes, dates, names, causes, or results. If a section lacks support, write [NEEDS FACT] and explain what information is missing. Keep the tone direct and specific. Do not make the client sound helpless or make our work sound magical.” Then paste the fact file underneath the prompt. The instruction to mark missing information is especially useful. It turns uncertainty into a visible editing task instead of a hidden error. Shape the story around decisions Once you have a draft, look for the decisions that make your work distinct. Many weak case studies read like timelines: first this happened, then that happened, then the project ended. A stronger version explains why a step mattered. For example, “we revised the intake form” is a task. “We revised the intake form so the first conversation could focus on the client’s priorities instead of collecting the same background information twice” explains the reasoning. The second sentence gives a reader a way to picture your method. Ask the AI to identify three to five moments where your judgment affected the work. Have it return each moment in this format: What information was available? What choice did you make? Why did that choice fit the situation? What happened afterward? Review the answers yourself. The tool can help you see patterns in your notes, but you are the person who knows whether the explanation is fair and complete. Separate outcomes from promises Be precise about what the project produced. A completed deliverable is different from a business result. A client saying that a process felt clearer is different from a verified revenue claim. A faster handoff may be an observation, but it should not become a precise time-saving statistic unless you have support for that number. Ask the AI to sort claims into three groups: Documented: Directly supported by your notes, records, or approved feedback. Reasonable interpretation: A possible explanation that still needs your judgment. Unsupported: A claim that should be removed or verified. Delete the third group. Rewrite the second group with careful language or remove it as well. You can still create an engaging story without promising that every future client will receive the same outcome. Run a human review before sharing Use a five-pass review instead of trying to catch every issue at once. Fact pass: Check names, dates, sequence, deliverables, and every number. Permission pass: Confirm that the client, project, screenshots, quotes, and identifying details can be used. Clarity pass: Remove internal jargon and explain any necessary term in plain language. Specificity pass: Replace vague praise with concrete actions and decisions. Voice pass: Make the wording sound like you, not like a generic marketing page. You can ask AI to perform each pass, but keep the source fact file beside the draft. If the tool suggests a correction, verify it against your records. Never accept a polished sentence just because it sounds convincing. Turn one approved case study into more content After the case study is approved, ask AI to create smaller pieces from the same source. Request one email that teaches the main lesson, three short posts that each explain one decision, a proposal paragraph describing your approach, and a list of questions a prospective client might ask. Keep the original case study as the source of truth. Every shorter piece should point back to the approved facts, and each format should have a different job. The email can teach. The posts can start conversations. The proposal can explain fit. None of them should stretch the original story into a promise you did not make. This workflow also gives you a repeatable habit: finish the project, capture the facts while they are fresh, draft the structure, review the claims, request permission, and then repurpose the approved version. You are building a library of useful proof one completed project at a time. The simple prompt sequence Save these four prompts in your working document: “Extract the facts, decisions, deliverables, supported outcomes, and open questions from these project notes. Do not fill gaps.” “Build a case-study outline for a prospective client. Center the outline on the problem, our decisions, and the method.” “Draft the outline using only supported information. Mark every missing fact instead of guessing.” “Audit this draft for unsupported claims, privacy risks, vague language, and statements that sound like guarantees.” That is enough to create a dependable first draft without handing over your judgment. AI can help you find the story inside your project notes. Your job is to decide what is true, what is permitted, and what would genuinely help the next person choose to work with you. If you want a larger system for turning your knowledge into consistent business content and follow-up, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: What should I give an AI tool before asking it to write a case study?
A: Give it your project notes, the original problem, the steps you took, approved facts, and any wording or details that must stay private. Tell it to mark missing information instead of guessing.

Q: Can AI write a case study without client results?
A: Yes. You can write about the starting problem, your method, decisions, deliverables, and lessons learned. Leave out performance claims until you have permission and support for them.

Q: How do I keep an AI-written case study accurate?
A: Compare every specific claim with your source notes, remove guesses, check names and dates, and have the appropriate person approve any client-facing details before publication.

Q: Where can I use the finished case study?
A: You can adapt it into a website article, sales follow-up, proposal example, email, presentation, or a short set of educational posts after reviewing the permissions and facts.

# How to Use AI to Build a Client Onboarding Checklist

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-client-onboarding-checklist
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-07-31T13:56:03.269Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A new client should not have to guess what happens after they say yes. Here is a simple way to use AI to turn your intake details into a useful onboarding checklist without handing over your judgment.

Use AI to turn your approved client intake notes into a first-week checklist, then review it before it reaches the client. The goal is not to let AI decide how you serve someone. The goal is to make sure small but meaningful steps do not disappear between the sale and the start of the work. That gap creates unnecessary uncertainty. A client says yes, you celebrate, and then the work gets mixed into email, calendar reminders, and a few notes in different places. You know what needs to happen, but your client may not. A clear onboarding checklist gives both of you a shared starting point. Why client onboarding gets messy Onboarding usually contains several kinds of work at once. You need to collect information, confirm expectations, schedule the first meeting, prepare materials, create access, and explain what the client should do next. None of those steps is especially difficult. The problem is that they are easy to handle differently every time. That inconsistency can create avoidable questions: What should I send first? Which details am I still waiting for? What does the client need to complete? Who owns the next action? When does the actual service begin? AI is useful here because it can organize a messy set of approved notes into a structure you can inspect. It can group tasks, find missing fields, and draft plain-language instructions. You still decide what is accurate, appropriate, and aligned with your offer. Start with a repeatable base checklist Before you ask AI to create a client-specific checklist, write down the steps that should happen for nearly every client. Keep this list practical. It might include: Confirm the signed agreement and payment status in your normal records. Send a welcome message with the next appointment or milestone. Collect the information or files required to begin. Share the communication channel and expected response times. Prepare the first deliverable, meeting agenda, or review. Confirm the client's first action and your first action. Schedule a check-in to confirm that the work is on track. This list becomes your starting point. It does not need to cover every possible situation. A useful base checklist is short enough to follow and specific enough to prevent missed handoffs. If the process changes often, document it as an SOP first. You can read more about turning a repeated task into an SOP in this AI SOP workflow . Give AI the right context AI can only organize the material you provide. Before you paste anything into a tool, decide what information is approved for that tool and remove details that are not needed for the task. You usually do not need every private note, internal opinion, or sensitive identifier to create a checklist. A useful input can contain: The service or package the client purchased. The client's stated goal in their own words. The agreed start date or first milestone. Required forms, documents, links, or access. Known preferences about meetings or communication. Your base onboarding checklist. You can also include a short instruction such as: “Organize these approved notes into an onboarding checklist. Separate client tasks from business tasks. Add an owner, a suggested timing, and a short reason for each step. Do not invent missing details. Mark anything that needs confirmation.” That final instruction matters. A polished sentence is not proof that the underlying detail is correct. Asking AI to mark uncertainty gives you a review list instead of hidden assumptions. Ask for four useful outputs One large paragraph is hard to use. Ask AI for outputs that match the way you actually work. 1. An internal task list Ask for a table or numbered list of your tasks. Each item should have an action, an owner, a timing, and a status field. For example, “prepare the kickoff agenda,” “Krista,” “before the first call,” and “not started” are more useful than a vague note that says “get ready.” 2. A client-facing checklist Ask AI to rewrite only the steps the client needs to see. Use direct language and explain what happens after each action. A client should be able to scan the list and know what to do first, what can wait, and where to ask for help. 3. A missing-information list Ask AI to separate missing information from optional information. This keeps you from sending a long questionnaire when you only need two answers to begin. 4. A welcome message Ask for a short message that confirms the decision, names the first milestone, and points to the checklist. Then edit it so it sounds like you. The welcome message should feel like a clear handoff, not an automated receipt. If the checklist begins with inquiry details, your qualification process can provide a cleaner starting point. See this guide to qualifying new business inquiries with AI for a related workflow. Review the draft before it becomes a promise Your review is the most important part of the process. Check every date, name, deliverable, permission, and expectation. Remove steps that do not belong to this client. Add the personal detail that shows you heard what they said. Look for four common problems: Invented details: AI may fill a gap with a plausible but unapproved assumption. Wrong ownership: A task may be assigned to the client when you should handle it, or the reverse. Too much work at once: A complete list can feel heavy if every later step appears on day one. Unclear language: Terms that make sense to you may not make sense to a new client. Ask yourself one simple question: if I were the client, would I know my next action after reading this? If the answer is no, shorten the list and make the first step more visible. Make the first week feel calm A good onboarding checklist is not a dump of every task in the engagement. It is a sequence. Put the earliest decision or action at the top. Group later work under headings such as “Before we meet,” “Our first meeting,” and “After the first milestone.” Keep the client-facing version focused on movement. Your internal version can contain more detail, including quality checks and preparation notes. This separation lets you run a careful process without asking the client to manage your entire back office. You can use AI again after the first meeting. Give it the meeting notes and ask it to compare the agreed next steps with the original checklist. It can identify what changed and draft an updated task list for your review. For a related notes workflow, read how to turn notes into a client-ready proposal . Turn the checklist into a system you can improve After several clients, review where the process still creates questions. Did people miss the same form? Did you explain a milestone too late? Did you spend time rewriting the same welcome message? Update the base checklist when a repeated improvement becomes clear. Keep a short “client-specific” section for details that should not be added to the standard process. This gives you consistency without making every person feel processed. You can also prepare a few approved prompt templates: one for the internal list, one for the client version, one for missing information, and one for the welcome message. Store them with your process so you are not rebuilding the request each time. AI will not replace the judgment that makes onboarding good. It can help you gather the pieces, expose gaps, and produce a first draft quickly. Your job is to make the final checklist accurate, kind, and easy to act on. When a client knows what happens next, you spend less time answering preventable questions and more time doing the work they hired you to do. If you want a larger system for using AI across your business, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should an AI-generated client onboarding checklist include?
A: It should include the client information you need, the actions your team must take, deadlines, owners, communication points, and the first meaningful milestone.

Q: Can AI send the onboarding checklist to my client?
A: AI can help draft the checklist and the accompanying message. You should review the details and send it through the system you already use.

Q: What information should I give AI for onboarding?
A: Give it approved intake details, the service purchased, known goals, timing, required documents, and your standard first-week steps. Remove information that should not be shared.

Q: How do I keep the checklist from sounding generic?
A: Include the client's stated goal, use your normal language, add a few specific next steps, and ask AI to flag anything that needs your confirmation.

Q: Should I create one checklist for every client?
A: Start with one repeatable base checklist, then let AI suggest a short client-specific section based on the approved intake information.
