# How to Use AI to Prepare for a Difficult Client Conversation

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-prepare-difficult-client-conversation
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-07-30T13:53:12.533Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A difficult client conversation gets easier when you separate facts from assumptions and decide what a useful outcome looks like before you speak. This practical AI workflow helps you prepare a clear conversation plan while keeping the relationship and your judgment at the center.

Use AI as a calm preparation partner. Give it an anonymized summary of the agreement, the timeline, what happened, what the client said, and the outcome you want. Ask it to separate facts from assumptions, identify unanswered questions, and help you rehearse a clear conversation. Then make the final decisions yourself. A difficult conversation is rarely difficult because you lack words. It is difficult because you are carrying too many versions of the situation at once. You may feel blamed, rushed, embarrassed, or worried about losing the relationship. When you prepare with those feelings still tangled together, you can overexplain, avoid the real issue, or promise something you cannot deliver. AI can help you sort the material before you walk into the conversation. It cannot know the full relationship, and it should not replace your judgment. Its job is to help you see the situation clearly enough to show up as the business owner your client needs. Start with a private, factual conversation brief Open a blank document and write the situation in plain language. Do not try to sound polished. Use notes such as: What the client hired me to do What was agreed about timing, communication, or deliverables What has happened so far What the client is concerned about What I am concerned about What I can change, clarify, or complete What I cannot promise Remove names, account numbers, addresses, health information, financial details, passwords, and anything else the tool does not need. If a detail identifies the client, replace it with a general label such as “the buyer,” “the coaching client,” or “the consulting customer.” The clearer your brief, the less likely you are to ask AI to fill gaps with guesses. Try this prompt: “Act as a conversation-preparation coach. Review the anonymized notes below. Create four sections: confirmed facts, assumptions I may be making, questions I need to ask, and issues that need a decision. Do not invent details or assign blame. Keep the language plain. Here are the notes: [paste notes].” Read the response slowly. The most useful line may be a question you had not considered. The least useful line may be a confident interpretation based on a missing fact. Keep the first and discard the second. Decide what a good conversation needs to accomplish Do not enter the call with the vague goal of “fixing everything.” Choose one or two outcomes that are within your control. You might need to understand the concern, correct a misunderstanding, agree on a next step, reset a boundary, or decide that the engagement should end. Ask AI to help you turn the situation into a small outcome statement: “Based on these facts, suggest three realistic outcomes for this conversation. For each one, list what I can control, what I need from the client, and what would remain unresolved. Do not recommend a promise unless the notes support it.” Then choose the outcome that fits your role and your agreement. AI can show you options, but you are the person who has to keep the promise after the call. A smaller, clear next step is usually more useful than a dramatic statement about making the entire problem disappear. Plan the conversation in five parts Once you know the outcome, create a short structure. A five-part plan works well for many client conversations: Open with respect. Thank the client for raising the issue and state that you want to understand it clearly. Name the shared topic. Say what you are there to discuss without labeling the client or defending yourself. Ask and listen. Use one question at a time. Let the client finish before you explain. Reflect the facts. Summarize what you heard and correct only what is inaccurate or incomplete. Agree on the next step. State who will do what, by when, and what still needs a decision. You can ask AI to turn your notes into this structure: “Create a conversation outline using these five parts: respectful opening, shared topic, questions, factual summary, and next step. Keep it warm and direct. Avoid blame, legal conclusions, promises, and corporate language. Use placeholders where a fact is missing.” Do not copy the outline word for word. Mark the two sentences you would actually say. The rest is there to keep you oriented if the conversation becomes emotional. Use AI to rehearse without losing your voice Rehearsal is where the workflow becomes practical. Ask AI to play the client and raise one concern at a time. Start with the concern you expect, then try a version that is more emotional or less specific. Your goal is not to win a debate. Your goal is to practice staying curious, precise, and honest. Use a prompt like this: “Role-play as a concerned client using only the facts in these notes. Ask one question at a time and wait for my response. After each response, give brief feedback on whether I was clear, defensive, vague, or specific. Do not add facts that are not in the notes.” After the rehearsal, ask for three edits: Which sentence sounded defensive? Where did I answer a question the client did not ask? What important question did I avoid? Keep your own words in the final version. Your client does not need a perfect speech. They need to understand what you heard, what is true, and what happens next. If AI produces language you would never use, replace it. A polished sentence that feels false can damage trust faster than a simple sentence with your natural voice. Turn the call into a written next step Before the conversation ends, repeat the agreement out loud. Afterward, write a short follow-up that includes the issue discussed, the decision made, the action owner, and the date or condition for the next check-in. You can use AI to organize your notes after removing identifying details. “Turn these anonymized meeting notes into a concise follow-up email. Include what we understood, what we agreed, who owns each action, and what remains open. Do not add commitments, dates, or explanations that are not in the notes.” Read every line before sending. Check names, dates, deliverables, and tone. If the email says something you did not agree to, delete it. If the conversation involved a safety issue, regulated advice, a legal dispute, or a material financial decision, pause and get the appropriate human guidance before relying on a generated draft. Build this into your business rhythm You do not need a complicated system. Save one conversation-preparation template with these headings: Situation Confirmed facts Open questions Desired outcome Conversation outline Promises I can keep Follow-up owner and next step When a concern arrives, spend a few minutes filling in the template before replying. If the same type of conversation happens repeatedly, document the human decisions that matter and create an SOP you can improve over time. If the issue came from a call, you can also connect the preparation notes to your normal transcript and next-action process. The point is not to make every client conversation sound the same. The point is to give yourself enough structure that stress does not make the decision for you. AI can help you sort, question, and rehearse. You bring the context, the responsibility, and the final word. If you want a larger set of practical workflows for using AI across your business, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI decide what I should say to an unhappy client?
A: AI can help you organize the situation, suggest questions, and rehearse possible wording. You should decide what is true, what you can offer, and what is appropriate for the relationship.

Q: What information should I give AI before a client conversation?
A: Give it a short, anonymized summary of the agreement, timeline, facts, open questions, and the outcome you want. Leave out sensitive personal information that the tool does not need.

Q: Should I send an AI-written apology to a client?
A: Read and rewrite it yourself. An apology needs to match what happened and what you are willing to do next, so generic language can make the conversation feel less personal.

Q: How can I use AI without sounding defensive?
A: Ask AI to remove blame, assumptions, and long explanations. Then keep the parts that sound like you and use the result as a conversation guide rather than a script.

# How to Use AI to Turn Client Questions Into Better Content

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-client-questions-content-plan
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-07-29T14:00:14.830Z
Author: Krista Mashore

The best content topics are often hiding in the questions people already ask you. Here is a practical AI workflow for turning those questions into clear content your audience can use.

Use AI to turn a real client question into a content plan, then add your judgment before you publish. The useful workflow is simple: collect the question, clarify the person asking it, generate a few angles, choose one answer, and turn that answer into several formats. This works because you are starting with a problem that already exists in a conversation. You are not sitting in front of a blank screen trying to guess what your audience wants. A coach can use a question about getting consistent leads. A lender can use a question about preparing for a loan conversation. A real estate agent can use a question about deciding whether to move. A consultant can use a question about what happens after the first call. The goal is not to have AI pretend to be the expert. The goal is to give your expertise a repeatable path from conversation to useful teaching. Start with the exact question Keep a running question list in one simple place. Add questions from calls, emails, direct messages, sales conversations, comments, and your own notes. Write the question as close to the original wording as you can. “How do I get more clients?” is a topic. “What should I do this week if I have no new inquiries?” is a working question. The second version gives you a person, a moment, and a decision to address. Before asking AI for ideas, remove private details that do not belong in a public article. Keep the business problem, the context needed to understand it, and the outcome the person wants. You can also add three short notes: Who is asking? What have they already tried? What decision do they need to make? Those notes give the draft a place to stand. Without them, AI may produce a broad answer that could apply to almost anyone. Use AI for angles before you ask for a draft Paste the question and your notes into your chosen AI tool. Ask for five possible teaching angles, not an article. Request a different job for each angle, such as a checklist, a common mistake, a first-week plan, a decision guide, or a short example. You can use a prompt like this: “I help [audience] with [specific problem]. A person asked: [exact question]. Their context is: [three notes]. Give me five useful content angles. Each angle should answer one practical part of the question, avoid hype, and make clear what the reader can do next. Do not write the article yet.” Read the five angles as an editor. Pick the one that matches your actual experience and the reader's immediate need. If every angle feels general, add more context instead of asking for a longer draft. Tell the tool what your process looks like, what you would ask first, and what you would not recommend. This small pause matters. A draft built from the wrong angle can be polished and still miss the question. Build the answer around a decision Once you choose an angle, give AI a clear structure. A practical business article often needs five parts: State the direct answer in the opening. Explain why the problem happens or why the decision matters. Give a short sequence of steps. Show how to adapt the steps to one business situation. End with a next action the reader can take today. Ask for headings and a rough outline first. Then add your own notes under each heading. These notes can be rough. Write the phrase you would say on a call, a warning you give often, or a question you ask before recommending a solution. After that, ask AI to draft from the outline. Set useful boundaries: write to one person, use plain language, keep the answer specific, and mark any place where more information is needed. Do not ask it to invent a result, quote, case study, or authority you did not provide. Add your voice in the editing pass AI can arrange information, but your point of view is what makes the piece worth reading. Read the draft aloud and look for sentences you would never say. Replace them. Add a small detail from your working method. Explain a tradeoff. Tell the reader what to do first and what to leave for later. Use this editing checklist: Does the first paragraph answer the question directly? Can the reader tell who the advice is for? Does every section help with a decision or action? Have broad claims been replaced with steps or examples? Did you remove private information and unsupported promises? Does the language sound like something you would say? Ask AI to act as a careful editor after you revise. Give it the draft and request a list of unclear sections, repeated ideas, and questions a beginner may still have. Ask for feedback only. Make the final choices yourself. Turn one answer into a small content set When the main piece is finished, reuse the thinking inside it. Ask AI to pull out three short lessons, one objection, one checklist, and one question for a conversation. Then adapt those pieces for the places where your audience already pays attention. For example, one article about responding to a quiet week could become a short post about the first action to take, an email about reviewing recent conversations, a video outline about what to stop doing, and a simple checklist for the next seven days. Each piece should have its own opening and should point back to the same useful answer. Do not copy every sentence into every format. The idea stays consistent, but the format changes. A social post may ask one sharp question. An email can explain the reasoning. A video can show the sequence. This is how one real conversation can support a week of communication without forcing you to invent a new topic every day. Make the workflow repeatable Save the steps as a short standard operating procedure. Include where questions come from, how you remove private details, the prompt you use for angles, the review questions, and the formats you create at the end. Set a regular time to review the question list. Choose one question that is specific, useful, and connected to the work you want to be known for. If a question is too broad, narrow it before you open the AI tool. Over time, this creates a library of answers that reflect the questions your audience actually brings you. It also gives you a clearer view of the subjects where your teaching is strongest and the places where your process needs more definition. Start with one question from this week. Give AI the real context, choose one angle, write from your experience, and edit until the answer sounds like you. If you want a larger system for turning your knowledge into consistent business communication, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: What kind of client questions should I give to AI?
A: Start with questions people ask before they buy, questions that reveal confusion, and questions that come up repeatedly in calls, emails, or conversations. Specific questions usually create stronger content than broad topics.

Q: Should AI write the whole article from one question?
A: It can create a draft, but a better process is to ask for several useful angles first. Then choose one angle, add your experience and examples, and edit the language so the final piece sounds like you.

Q: How do I keep AI content from sounding generic?
A: Give AI a real audience, a clear point of view, details from your process, and words you actually use. Then remove vague claims and replace them with practical steps, choices, and examples.

Q: Can this workflow create social posts too?
A: Yes. After the main piece is edited, ask AI to identify its strongest lessons and adapt them into short posts, an email, or a video outline. Review each version before publishing.

# How to Use AI to Turn Notes Into a Client-Ready Proposal

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-notes-client-ready-proposal
Pillar: AI Content to Client System
Published: 2026-07-28T14:12:38.783Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Rough notes are enough to start a strong proposal when you give AI a clear job and your own judgment stays in charge. This workflow helps you organize the client's situation, shape the offer, and edit the final document so it sounds like you.

Yes, you can turn rough notes into a client-ready proposal with AI, but the quality depends on the information and judgment you bring to the process. Use AI to sort the conversation, identify the client's real need, create a first structure, and point out missing details. Then you make the promises, set the scope, and edit every important sentence. This is useful after a discovery call, consultation, property conversation, audit, or strategy session. Instead of staring at a blank page, you begin with a working draft that reflects what was discussed. The goal isn't to hand your thinking to a tool. The goal is to give your thinking a clean path to the client. The five-part AI proposal workflow A proposal usually needs to answer five questions: What did you hear? What problem are you solving? What will you do? What does the client need to provide? What happens next? Ask AI to organize those answers, not to make up a sales pitch. 1. Gather the source notes Start with the notes you already have. These might be your handwritten notes, a typed summary, a transcript, or a follow-up email. Remove information that does not belong in the proposal, especially private details that aren't needed to explain the work. Before you paste anything into an AI tool, check that you have permission to use the material in that setting. Replace names or identifying details when they aren't necessary. A proposal can be specific without repeating every personal detail from a conversation. Your notes should contain as many of these items as possible: The client's current situation The outcome the client wants The obstacles or limits you discussed The service or approach you believe fits Any agreed timing, budget range, or decision process The next action each person is expected to take If a detail is unknown, write “not confirmed” instead of guessing. That small habit gives you a much safer starting point. 2. Ask AI to separate facts from gaps Your first prompt should be a sorting prompt. Tell the tool to use only the notes provided. Ask it to create four sections: confirmed facts, client goals, proposed solution, and questions that still need an answer. You can use this prompt as a starting point: “Read these business notes and use only the information included. Organize them into confirmed facts, the client's stated goals, possible service needs, and missing information. Do not invent prices, dates, deliverables, credentials, or results. Quote uncertain points as questions for me to confirm.” This step gives you a chance to correct the source before a polished draft hides the gaps. If the notes say the client wants “more leads,” you may need to clarify whether that means inquiries, booked calls, applications, or something else. A proposal built around a vague outcome creates confusion later. 3. Choose the promise and the boundaries Now decide what you are actually offering. Keep the proposal focused on one primary outcome and a clear set of activities. If you provide several services, explain which one is the first step and what would be outside the current scope. Ask AI to turn your decisions into a plain-language outline with these sections: Opening summary of the client's situation Desired outcome Recommended approach Specific deliverables Client responsibilities Timing and decision points Investment and payment terms, if confirmed Next step Don't ask for “the best proposal.” Ask for an accurate proposal based on your confirmed decisions. Those are different instructions. The first invites decoration. The second protects the substance. 4. Draft in your natural voice Give the tool a short description of your voice. You might say that you write in a direct, warm style, use short paragraphs, explain unfamiliar terms, and avoid pressure. You can also provide a few sentences you have written yourself as a reference. Then ask for a draft that speaks to one person. The opening should show that you understood the client's situation. It shouldn't begin with a long description of your company. Put the client's need first, then explain how your work addresses it. Watch for vague language such as “take your business to the next level” or “get amazing results.” Replace it with observable work. For example, “I will review your current inquiry process, write a response sequence, and create a checklist for weekly follow-up” tells the client what they will receive. You can also ask AI to produce two versions of a section: one concise and one more conversational. Choose the version that sounds closest to you, then edit it yourself. Your edits are what turn a generic draft into a real proposal. 5. Review before you send Read the proposal as if you were the client. Can you tell what is included? Can you tell what is not included? Is the next step easy to find? Does every claim match your notes and your actual offer? Use a final review prompt such as: “Review this proposal against the source notes. List every sentence that contains an unsupported fact, an unclear promise, a missing decision, or an ambiguous deliverable. Do not rewrite it yet. Show me what I need to verify.” After you answer those questions, ask for a clean copy. Still, don't rely on the review prompt alone. Check names, numbers, dates, links, attachments, pricing, and spelling with your own eyes. Make sure the proposal doesn't include internal comments or instructions meant only for you. What makes a proposal feel personal Personal writing comes from accurate listening, not from adding more adjectives. Include one or two details that show you heard the client's concern. Connect your recommendation to the stated goal. Explain why the first step makes sense for this situation. Keep the tone calm and specific. You don't need to create urgency that the client didn't express. You also don't need to promise an outcome you cannot control. A useful proposal makes the decision clearer by showing the work, the boundaries, and the path to begin. One practical test is to read the proposal out loud. If a sentence sounds like something you would never say on a call, change it. If the document could describe almost any business, add the concrete details that belong to this client. Turn the workflow into a repeatable system Save the structure as a reusable template, but keep the source notes and final proposal separate. Your template can contain the sections, review questions, and voice guidance. Each new proposal should begin with fresh notes and confirmed facts. After you send it, record what happened. Did the client ask about scope? Was a section unclear? Did you spend too long checking a certain detail? Those observations can improve your template. You can also connect this workflow to the work you do after a discovery call, then create a simple follow-up process for proposals that are still awaiting a decision. AI is most helpful here when it handles the blank page and the sorting. You remain responsible for the relationship, the offer, and the promises. That division of work can help you respond faster while keeping the proposal grounded in what you actually heard and what you can actually deliver. If you want a larger system for using AI across content, follow-up, and daily business operations, learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI write a proposal from a short set of notes?
A: Yes, if the notes include the client's situation, desired outcome, constraints, and your proposed next step. AI can organize gaps, but you should supply missing facts and make the final decisions.

Q: How do I keep an AI-written proposal personal?
A: Give AI a few examples of how you explain your work, then revise the draft with specific observations from the conversation. Remove generic promises and phrases you would not say aloud.

Q: What should I never let AI invent in a proposal?
A: Do not let it invent prices, deadlines, deliverables, guarantees, credentials, client facts, or expected results. Mark any missing item and confirm it yourself.

Q: Should I send the AI draft without reviewing it?
A: No. Read the entire proposal for accuracy, tone, scope, privacy, and clear expectations before you send it. The draft saves time, but your review protects the relationship.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Messy Inbox Into a Daily Action List

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-messy-inbox-daily-action-list
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-07-27T14:02:57.812Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A crowded inbox can make your whole business feel urgent. This practical AI workflow helps you sort messages into decisions, replies, follow-ups, and reference material so you can begin the day with a clear list.

Yes, you can use AI to turn a messy inbox into a useful daily action list, but you should use it as a sorting assistant, not as the person in charge of your business. Give it a defined batch of messages, a few categories, and your rules for urgency. Then review the result before you act. Your inbox is not a plan. It is a collection of requests, updates, questions, reminders, receipts, and conversations. When every message looks equally urgent, you spend the first part of the day deciding what deserves your attention. A short AI sorting step can make that decision easier. A simple inbox-to-action workflow The workflow has five parts: collect, remove sensitive details, classify, reduce, and review. It works for an entrepreneur, coach, consultant, real estate agent, lender, solopreneur, or creator because it is based on the shape of the work rather than a particular email app. 1. Collect a manageable batch Start with the messages that are still unresolved. You don't need to process your entire inbox at once. A batch of 10 to 20 messages is enough to create a useful first list. Copy the subject line and the relevant message text into your AI conversation. Include the date and any context that changes the decision, such as a promised deadline or a scheduled conversation. If you already use labels, group messages by label before you paste them. Don't include every footer, signature, tracking notice, or old thread. The goal is to show the request and the information needed to decide what happens next. 2. Protect private information Before you share message text, remove information that isn't needed for the task. That may include a client's full name, phone number, street address, financial account details, login information, or any other sensitive detail. Replace it with simple labels such as [CLIENT], [PROPERTY], or [VENDOR]. If you aren't sure whether a message should be shared, don't paste it. Summarize the situation instead: “A past client asked whether I can recommend a contractor for a small repair.” AI can still help you decide on a next step without seeing the person's identity. 3. Use four clear categories Give each message one primary category. Four categories are enough for most daily sorting: Reply today: Someone needs an answer or a decision from you. Schedule or delegate: The work belongs on your calendar or can be assigned to someone else. Waiting: You have already taken your step and need another person to respond. Reference: The message contains information you may need, but no action is required now. These categories are practical because each one leads to a different behavior. Reply today becomes a focused writing block. Schedule or delegate becomes a calendar or assignment. Waiting becomes a follow-up reminder. Reference leaves your immediate list. 4. Ask for decisions, not a summary A summary can sound helpful while leaving you with the same problem: you still have to decide what to do. Ask AI to recommend the next action for each message. You can use a prompt like this: “Sort these inbox messages into reply today, schedule or delegate, waiting, or reference. For each message, write the one next action in eight words or fewer. Mark the top three actions for today. Explain the reason for each top-three choice using only the information provided. If a deadline is not stated, write ‘no deadline provided’ instead of guessing.” The last instruction matters. A message may feel urgent because of its tone, but urgency should come from a real deadline, a business consequence you have defined, or a commitment you already made. If the information isn't there, the answer should say so. 5. Review the list before you trust it AI can organize the information you give it, but it doesn't know every commitment in your head. Check the three highlighted actions against your calendar, current projects, client promises, and cash-producing work. Ask yourself three questions: Does this action belong to me, or should I assign it? What is the actual deadline or consequence? What is the smallest next step that gets this moving? Then rewrite the list in your own task system. Keep the final version short. Three important actions, two quick replies, and one follow-up block may be enough for a full day. How to make the daily list more useful Give AI your work rules The quality of the sorting improves when your rules are specific. Tell AI what counts as a priority in your business. For example, you might say that a scheduled client conversation outranks a general networking request, or that a message related to an active transaction should be reviewed before a newsletter. Don't write a long policy on the first attempt. Begin with three rules. Test them for a week. Keep the rules that help you make decisions and remove the ones that create extra debate. Separate real work from inbox maintenance A reply is not always the most valuable action. Some messages are easy to answer but distract you from work that creates a better customer experience or advances a current opportunity. Ask AI to add a second label for the kind of work involved: client service, sales, delivery, administration, or personal. This lets you see whether your day is being filled by maintenance instead of the work your business needs. Turn repeated decisions into a procedure If you sort the same kind of message every week, write down the rule. A repeated decision can become a short standard operating procedure that you or a team member can follow. For example, a procedure for a new consultation inquiry might say: check whether the person included a service need, location, and preferred timing; record missing details; send the approved response; and set a follow-up reminder. Your AI assistant can then help you apply the procedure consistently. For a related process, see how to turn a repeated task into an SOP . Use a waiting list, not memory Waiting messages are easy to lose because they feel finished. Ask AI to extract the person or organization you are waiting on, the item you need, and a suggested check-in date only when a real date or your own follow-up rule supports it. Review that waiting list during your weekly business review. You can pair this workflow with an AI-assisted weekly review so open loops have a regular place to surface. What not to hand over Don't let AI send messages, make promises, approve refunds, interpret a contract, give financial or legal advice, or decide how to handle a sensitive personal situation without your review. Keep those decisions with the person who has the context and responsibility. Don't ask it to invent a deadline, infer a customer's intent as fact, or fill gaps with a confident guess. A clean list built on an incorrect assumption is more dangerous than a messy inbox. When a message relates to a lead, AI can help identify missing information and suggest a follow-up question. You can then compare that process with a practical inquiry qualification workflow . When a message follows a meeting, a transcript-based process may be a better fit than inbox sorting, as shown in this guide to turning a discovery call into next actions . Your five-minute daily reset At the start of the day, select a small batch of unresolved messages. Remove unnecessary private details, give AI your four categories and three priority rules, and ask for the top three actions. Review the result against your calendar and commitments. Move the final actions into your task system, then close the AI conversation until your next review. The point isn't to answer more email. It's to make fewer decisions while staring at an undifferentiated pile of requests. A clear daily list gives your attention somewhere specific to go. If you want a larger system for using AI across content, follow-up, and business operations, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI organize my inbox without sending anything?
A: Yes. You can give AI a copied batch of messages or a short summary and ask it to sort, label, and prioritize them without drafting or sending a reply. Keep the final decision and sending step with you.

Q: What should I do if an email contains private information?
A: Remove names, account numbers, addresses, and other sensitive details before sharing text with an AI tool. You can also describe the situation in general terms and ask for a workflow instead of pasting the message.

Q: How many inbox categories should I use?
A: Start with four: reply today, schedule or delegate, waiting for someone else, and reference. A small set makes the daily list easier to use and maintain.

Q: How can I keep AI from making my list too long?
A: Give it a limit. Ask for the three most important actions, then place everything else in a later or waiting section with a reason for its placement.

Q: Should AI write every email reply for me?
A: No. Use it first to clarify the request, identify the next step, and suggest a concise draft when helpful. Review the facts, tone, promises, and recipients before sending.

# How to Use AI to Turn a Repeated Task Into an SOP

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-repeated-task-standard-operating-procedure
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-07-26T13:51:28.519Z
Author: Krista Mashore

If you do the same business task every week, you already have the raw material for a standard operating procedure. This practical AI workflow helps you capture the steps, test the instructions, and create an SOP someone else can follow.

Yes. The fastest way is to explain the task as you actually do it, ask AI to organize your explanation into a draft SOP, and then test that draft with a person who wasn't in your head while you wrote it. The goal isn't to make a polished document for its own sake. The goal is to remove repeated questions, protect the way you want the work done, and make the business less dependent on one person's memory. Most business owners don't have a documentation problem because they lack knowledge. They have one because the knowledge is scattered across habits, browser tabs, messages, and half-finished checklists. AI is useful here as a structure partner. You supply the real process. It helps you expose the order, decisions, missing details, and quality checks. Choose the right task to document Don't begin with the biggest process in your business. Begin with a repeated task that is small enough to finish and important enough to matter. You perform it at least once a week. It has a recognizable starting point and finished result. You answer the same questions about it more than once. Another person could do it if the instructions were clear. A missed step creates rework, delays, or an inconsistent customer experience. For example, you might document how you prepare a weekly marketing review, turn a call into follow-up actions, prepare a new lead for a consultation, or check a piece of content before it goes live. Pick one. A narrow SOP that gets used is more valuable than a giant operations manual that nobody opens. Capture the process before you ask AI to format it Open a plain document and describe the task in your own words. Don't try to sound professional. Write what you would tell a capable assistant sitting beside you. Include the trigger, the tools you open, the order of actions, the choices you make, the information you check, and the final handoff. If you skip a step because it feels obvious, mark it anyway. What feels obvious to you is often the exact step a new helper won't know. Use this simple capture format: Trigger: What tells you it is time to start? Inputs: What files, messages, records, or information do you need? Actions: What do you do, in order? Decisions: When do you choose one path over another? Quality check: How do you know the work is correct? Handoff: What happens next, and who needs the result? Write one real example as you go. If you say, “Review the request,” explain what you look for. If you say, “Send the follow-up,” explain what must be true before it goes out. Specific examples make the hidden rules visible. Use AI to find the gaps and build the first draft Once you have your rough notes, give them to your preferred AI tool with a focused request. Ask it to act as an operations editor, not as the owner of your business. That distinction matters because your draft is the source of truth. You can use a prompt like this: “Turn the process below into a practical SOP for a capable assistant. Keep the actual order of operations. Separate required steps from optional improvements. Identify any vague instructions, missing decisions, or undefined terms. Add a purpose, trigger, inputs, numbered steps, quality check, and handoff section. Do not invent tools, policies, or steps. Put questions for me at the end.” Then paste your notes. Review the questions before asking for a second draft. AI may notice that you never explained what counts as a complete record, where a file should be saved, or what to do when the normal path doesn't apply. Those are useful discoveries. Answer them from your real process instead of allowing guesses into the SOP. At this stage, ask AI to make the document easier to scan. Short steps, clear headings, and decision language help more than decorative wording. A person should be able to find the next action quickly while doing the work. Make decisions explicit The strongest SOPs explain what to do when the situation changes. A list of ideal steps isn't enough if the task regularly produces exceptions. Add simple “if this, then that” rules where they belong. For example: If the required information is missing, pause and request it before completing the next step. If the request falls outside the normal service, send it for review instead of promising an answer. If the final check fails, return to the specific step that caused the issue. If a record contains sensitive information, use the approved storage location and don't copy it into the working notes. Keep these rules tied to observable conditions. “Use good judgment” isn't an instruction. “If the name, contact method, or requested service is missing, mark the item incomplete and ask for the missing detail” gives someone a path. Test the SOP with a fresh set of eyes Never assume the document works because it reads well. Give it to someone who didn't create the task and ask them to follow it without a running explanation from you. Watch where they pause. Listen for questions. Notice which words they interpret differently. That test creates your revision list. You may need to define a tool name, add a screenshot reference, clarify ownership, or separate two actions that were written as one. Ask the tester to tell you what the finished result should look like. If they can't describe it, your quality check needs more detail. You can also ask AI to review the SOP from the perspective of a new assistant. Give it the draft and ask: “List every step where a person could reasonably make two different choices. For each one, explain what information would make the choice clear.” This is a practical way to find ambiguity, but you remain responsible for deciding the correct rule. Keep the SOP alive without making it complicated A process changes when your tools, offer, team, or customer experience changes. Add a small owner and review rule to the document. Write who maintains it and what event should trigger a review, such as a missed handoff, a repeated question, or a change to the system used in the process. Store one approved version in a place your team can find. Don't let five slightly different copies become the new source of confusion. When you update the SOP, note what changed in plain language and let the person using it know. After the first SOP works, repeat the method for the next task that creates friction. Over time, these documents become the operating memory of the business. They also give AI better material to work from when you need help creating checklists, training notes, follow-up drafts, or a review plan. Your next 30 minutes Choose one task you completed this week. Set a timer for 10 minutes and describe it without editing yourself. Spend the next 10 minutes asking AI to organize the notes and identify gaps. Use the last 10 minutes to remove invented details, add the missing decisions, and hand the draft to someone for a quick test. That's enough to create a useful first version. You don't need a perfect manual before you can make the next handoff easier. Start with the task that keeps returning to your desk, capture the way you really do it, and improve the instructions each time the process teaches you something. If you want a larger system for connecting AI workflows to the way your business creates authority, follows up, and serves people, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: What kind of task should I document first?
A: Start with a task you repeat often, has a clear beginning and end, and causes confusion when someone else tries to help. A weekly report, lead follow-up routine, content checklist, or client onboarding step can all work.

Q: Can AI write an SOP from a short description?
A: AI can create a useful first draft from a description, but the quality depends on the details you provide. You still need to review the draft against the real process and correct anything missing or out of order.

Q: How long should a small-business SOP be?
A: Make it long enough to remove the common points of confusion and no longer. A focused SOP may fit on one page, while a process with decisions, examples, and quality checks may need several sections.

Q: Should an SOP include passwords or private customer information?
A: No. Keep passwords, private records, payment details, and other sensitive information out of the document. Refer to the approved system or access process instead, and follow your own privacy and security rules.

Q: How do I know whether the SOP is ready?
A: Give the instructions to someone who did not create the process and ask them to complete the task. Every question or wrong turn is a signal to clarify the SOP.

# How to Use AI to Qualify New Business Inquiries

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-qualify-new-business-inquiries
Pillar: The Authority Agent Operating System™
Published: 2026-07-25T13:54:42.608Z
Author: Krista Mashore

AI can help you bring order to a new inquiry before you spend time writing a response. This practical workflow shows you how to extract the facts, spot the missing information, and prepare a human follow-up that moves the conversation ahead.

Use AI to qualify a new business inquiry by turning the message into a short fact sheet, comparing those facts with your fit criteria, identifying what is missing, and preparing one useful follow-up draft. AI should organize your thinking, not make the relationship feel like a form submission. That distinction matters because a new inquiry is both an opportunity and a signal. The person may be ready to buy, still deciding what they need, or simply asking a question. If you answer every inquiry the same way, you'll either spend too much time on poor-fit conversations or rush people who need a clearer next step. Start with a simple qualification definition Before you ask AI to review an inquiry, write down what a qualified conversation means in your business. Keep it practical. You might care about the person's problem, the service they are asking about, their desired timing, their location or market, and whether your way of working fits what they want. Don't start with a complicated scoring model. A short set of observable questions is easier to review and improve: What problem is this person trying to solve? What outcome did they ask for? What information did they volunteer? What important information is missing? What would make this a poor fit? What is the most helpful next step? Write your answers in plain language. “Needs a home valuation” is more useful than “high-intent prospect.” “Wants help this quarter” is more useful than “urgent.” Your AI workflow is only as clear as the criteria you give it. The five-part inquiry workflow 1. Paste the inquiry and ask for facts first Give AI the original inquiry and tell it not to draft a reply yet. Ask for a neutral summary using only information that appears in the message. Separate facts from assumptions. A useful instruction looks like this: “Read the inquiry below. Extract the person's stated problem, requested outcome, timing, relevant context, and questions. List unknowns separately. Do not guess intent, budget, urgency, or personal circumstances.” This first pass prevents a common mistake: treating a confident interpretation as if it came from the potential client. If the person says, “I need help getting more consistent leads,” that is the fact. “They are ready for a full marketing rebuild” is an assumption. 2. Compare the facts with your fit criteria Next, provide the short qualification definition you created. Ask AI to compare the inquiry with it and show the result as three groups: clear fit, unclear, and possible concern. For example, a consultant might define a clear fit as someone who has a specific business problem, wants hands-on guidance, and is willing to complete a defined next step. An inquiry that says, “I want a magic prompt that replaces my whole team today” may belong in the possible-concern group. That doesn't automatically mean you should reject the person. It tells you what to clarify. Ask for evidence beside each conclusion. The evidence should point back to the inquiry, not to a general theory about buyers. This makes the review easier for you to approve. 3. Create the smallest set of follow-up questions When an inquiry is incomplete, AI can produce a long list of questions. Don't send the list. Ask it to choose the two or three questions that will change your next decision. Good follow-up questions are specific and easy to answer. “What are your goals?” is broad. “Which part of your current follow-up process breaks down most often?” gives the person a clear place to begin. “What would you like to have working in the next 30 days?” helps establish a practical time frame without promising a result. Tell AI to avoid questions whose answers you already have. Repeating information makes your process feel careless, even when the rest of the message is warm. 4. Prepare a reply with a clear next step Now ask for a draft. Give it the facts, the unanswered questions, your tone guidance, and the next step you actually offer. The next step might be a short call, an application, a resource, or a direct answer. Don't ask AI to invent a process you don't run. A strong reply usually does four things: Recognizes the person's stated situation. Answers the question you can answer now. Asks only the most useful follow-up questions. Explains what happens next if they want help. Ask for one draft that is concise and one that is slightly warmer. Then combine them yourself. Your final edit is where judgment and personality return to the message. 5. Record the decision and improve the criteria After you respond, record a few simple fields in the place where you track inquiries: the problem, fit status, next step, owner, and follow-up date. You don't need a lengthy report. You need enough information to see whether your qualification definition is helping you make consistent decisions. At the end of each week, review a small group of inquiries. Which questions kept appearing? Which “possible concerns” turned out to be irrelevant? Which good-fit people stalled because the next step wasn't clear? Update the criteria and prompt based on what you learn. How to write the operating prompt Put the workflow into one reusable prompt. Include five sections: Role: “You are my inquiry review assistant.” Business context: what you sell, who you serve, and what you don't do. Fit criteria: the observable conditions for a useful conversation. Output format: facts, unknowns, fit notes, questions, and draft reply. Boundaries: don't guess, don't promise outcomes, don't make a final decision, and flag sensitive information. Keep the original inquiry separate from your instructions. Label it clearly. If you use a saved workspace for your business context, check that the instructions still reflect your current offer before relying on the output. You can also ask AI to return a “needs human review” flag when the message is ambiguous, emotional, legally sensitive, or outside your normal service. A flag is valuable because it tells you when the workflow has reached its limit. What this system should never do It shouldn't reject people based on guesses about their income, personality, identity, or seriousness. It shouldn't promise a sales result, provide professional advice outside your role, or send a message without your review. It also shouldn't store more personal information than your business needs for the next step. Think of AI as a second set of eyes for structure. You remain responsible for the standards, the relationship, and the decision. The system earns its place when it helps you respond with more care and less mental clutter. Make the next response easier to send A consistent inquiry workflow gives you a repeatable starting point without forcing every person into the same script. You know what was said, what is unknown, what matters for fit, and what action should happen next. Start with five recent inquiries. Run the fact-extraction step only. Correct the assumptions, then add your fit criteria and follow-up questions. Once the output reflects how you actually think, add the reply draft. That order keeps the system grounded in your judgment. If you want a larger operating system for using AI across authority, content, follow-up, and daily business decisions, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: Can AI decide whether a lead is a good fit?
A: AI can organize the information you have and compare it with criteria you provide. You should make the final fit decision, especially when the inquiry is incomplete or sensitive.

Q: What should I give AI when a new inquiry arrives?
A: Give it the inquiry text, your offer, your fit criteria, your boundaries, and the next step you want a qualified person to take. Remove private details that aren't needed.

Q: Should AI write the first reply?
A: It can prepare a draft, but review it before sending. The draft should sound like you, answer the person's actual question, and ask only for the information you still need.

Q: How do I keep this from sounding automated?
A: Ask AI to quote or refer to the person's specific situation, keep the message short, avoid claims you can't support, and leave room for your own final edit.

# How to Use AI for a Weekly Business Review

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-weekly-business-review-next-week-plan
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-07-24T13:56:12.101Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A weekly review can become a short, repeatable AI workflow instead of another task you postpone. Here is how to give AI the right information, ask better questions, and turn the conversation into a practical plan for next week.

Use AI as a thinking partner for your weekly business review. Give it a clean summary of what happened, what is unfinished, what matters next, and what limits your time. Then ask it to find patterns, expose tradeoffs, and turn your priorities into a short plan. You still make the decisions, but you no longer have to organize every thought from a blank page. This is useful when your week contains a little bit of everything: sales conversations, content, customer work, admin, family commitments, and ideas that keep arriving before the last ones are finished. Without a review, those items can all feel equally urgent. A focused AI conversation can help you see the difference between activity and progress. Start with a weekly review input sheet Do not begin by asking, “What should I do next week?” That question is too broad. First, collect the information AI needs to reason about your actual week. You can put the notes in a document, a spreadsheet, or a conversation with the tool you already use. Use these six headings: Wins: What moved forward, even if it was small? Completed work: What did you finish or deliver? Open loops: What is waiting for you, another person, or a decision? Signals: What did prospects, customers, your audience, or your numbers tell you? Friction: What took too long, repeated itself, or kept getting postponed? Constraints: How much time, energy, and support do you actually have next week? Keep the notes plain. A few honest lines under each heading are more useful than polished paragraphs. If a number matters to the decision, include the number and the period it covers. If a customer or prospect is involved, remove identifying details unless you have a clear reason and permission to share them. Ask AI to separate facts from interpretation Your notes will contain both what happened and what you think it means. Ask AI to keep those two categories separate before it suggests a plan. This small step can prevent a guess from quietly becoming a business decision. Try this prompt: “Review the notes below. Create two sections: confirmed observations and possible interpretations. Do not invent missing information. For each interpretation, name the evidence that supports it and what I would need to check. Then list the three decisions that would have the greatest effect on next week.” The phrase “do not invent missing information” matters. AI can produce a confident sentence when your notes are incomplete. You want it to show the gap instead. A useful review might say that several people asked about the same service, while treating the reason for that interest as a question to investigate. Read the response like a business owner, not like a report card. Correct anything that is wrong. Add context the notes missed. If the tool gives a recommendation based on an assumption, ask it to state that assumption in simple language. Turn the review into a short list of priorities Most weekly plans fail because they contain too many priorities. Ask AI to rank possible work using criteria that fit your business. For example, you might ask it to consider customer impact, revenue relevance, time required, deadlines, and whether the work creates a reusable asset. Use a prompt like this: “Using the confirmed observations, rank the possible tasks for next week. Score each task from one to five for customer impact, business value, urgency, and effort. Show the scores, explain where the judgment is uncertain, and recommend no more than three priorities. Treat the score as a discussion tool, not a final decision.” A score is not a fact. It is a way to make your choices visible. If AI ranks a low-effort task above an important relationship, you can change the criteria or reject the result. The benefit is not that a tool knows your perfect order. The benefit is that you can see why a crowded list is crowded. Build next week around outcomes Once you select your priorities, ask AI to rewrite them as outcomes with a clear finish line. “Work on my newsletter” is activity. “Send the Thursday newsletter to the approved list” is an outcome. “Follow up with leads” is vague. “Send a personal reply to the five people who requested a consultation” is easier to recognize as complete. For each priority, ask for: The result you want by the end of the week. The smallest first action. The next two or three steps. The time or information required. A definition of done. The one thing that could block it. Then ask AI to place those actions on a realistic calendar. Tell it when you are unavailable, how much time you can work, and which commitments cannot move. If you have only five focused hours for a project, the plan should not quietly assign twelve. Ask for a “minimum version” of every priority. This is especially helpful for content, sales follow-up, and internal projects. Your minimum version might be one useful email instead of a full campaign, or one decision about a process instead of a complete rebuild. A smaller finished result gives you information and keeps the next review grounded in what actually happened. Use AI to find repeated friction One review tells you what happened this week. Several reviews can show you what keeps happening. Save the weekly summaries in one place, then ask AI to compare them after you have enough notes to make the comparison meaningful. You could ask: “Compare these weekly reviews. Identify repeated unfinished tasks, recurring sources of delay, questions customers ask more than once, and work that appears to depend on me personally. Quote only from the notes provided. Group similar items and suggest one process change for each group.” Look for patterns you can address with a checklist, template, scheduled block, clearer offer, or delegated step. Do not create a new system for every inconvenience. Pick the repeated problem that costs you the most attention and test one change for a week. This is also where your review can connect to a broader AI operating system. A repeated question may become a content topic. A repeated follow-up may become a saved message and a reminder. A task that depends on your exact voice may need documented examples and review criteria before anyone else handles it. Finish with a five-minute commitment End the review by writing a compact commitment for yourself. Ask AI to return: My three priorities for next week. The first action for each priority. The appointment or work block where each action begins. The one task I will remove, delay, or decline. The question I should answer in next week’s review. Copy that final version into the place where you already check your schedule or task list. A plan hidden in an AI conversation is easy to forget. Keep the final output short enough to read at the beginning of each workday. On the next review, start by checking what you committed to and what changed. If a priority did not happen, ask what blocked it before adding it back. Sometimes the answer is a poor estimate. Sometimes the work was not important enough. Sometimes a new customer need took its place. Each answer gives you a better basis for the next plan. The rule that keeps this workflow useful AI should reduce the mental sorting around your business, not replace your judgment. Give it specific notes, require it to show uncertainty, limit the number of priorities, and make the final plan fit your real week. That is enough to turn a scattered Friday afternoon into a repeatable review. If you want a larger system for using AI across authority, content, follow-up, and daily operations, see the AI-run business pillar and then Learn the AI System .

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI for a weekly business review?
A: Give it your goals, completed work, open tasks, meaningful numbers, customer signals, and constraints for next week. Remove private information that is not needed for the planning question.

Q: Can AI decide my business priorities for me?
A: AI can sort information, point out tradeoffs, and suggest a sequence. You should make the final decisions because you know your commitments, customers, and risk better than a general-purpose tool does.

Q: How long should an AI weekly review take?
A: Set aside enough time to collect a useful input list and read the output carefully. The goal is a clear plan you will use, not a long report.

Q: What if I missed most of my goals this week?
A: Ask AI to separate a genuine priority from a crowded list, identify what blocked progress, and suggest one smaller next action. A review is for learning and choosing, not for producing a perfect score.

Q: Should my weekly review include personal tasks?
A: Include them when they affect your business capacity, schedule, or commitments. Keep the review focused on decisions and work that matter for the coming week.

# How to Turn a Discovery Call Transcript Into Your Next Actions

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/ai-discovery-call-transcript-next-actions
Pillar: The AI-Run Business
Published: 2026-07-23T23:33:22.890Z
Author: Krista Mashore

A discovery call transcript is only useful when it leads to a clear next step. Here is a simple AI workflow for turning a messy conversation into organized notes, follow-up, and a short task list.

Use AI to turn the transcript into four things: what the person wants, what you promised, what is still unknown, and the next actions with owners and dates. That gives you a useful record of the conversation instead of another block of text you may never open again. This workflow works for a discovery call with a coaching prospect, a seller, a borrower, a consulting lead, or a potential partner. The goal is not to have AI make the relationship feel automated. The goal is to remove the clerical work between a good conversation and a thoughtful follow-up. Start with the outcome you need Before you paste a transcript into an AI tool, decide what you want back. A vague request such as “summarize this call” often produces a vague summary. Ask for a decision-support document instead. Your request can be as simple as this: “Read this discovery call transcript and create a practical follow-up plan. Separate the prospect's stated goals, concerns, current situation, decision process, commitments I made, open questions, and next actions. Use only information in the transcript. Mark anything uncertain as unknown. Do not invent details.” That last instruction matters. A polished paragraph can still be wrong. You want a clear boundary between what was said, what you can reasonably infer, and what needs to be confirmed. The four-part transcript workflow 1. Pull out the person's actual priorities Ask AI to list the person's goals in their own language. Then ask it to separate a desired outcome from a surface request. Someone might ask about content, for example, while describing a larger problem with inconsistent leads or an overloaded calendar. Do not turn every comment into a business need. Have AI label each item as a stated goal, concern, constraint, or background detail. This keeps you from treating a casual remark as a promise or a buying signal. For a real estate conversation, the output might include a target move date, a concern about timing, and a question about preparation. For a consultant, it might include a team bottleneck, a desired result, and a limit on available hours. The exact categories matter less than keeping them visible and separate. 2. Create a promise and question ledger The second pass should focus on the parts of the conversation that create responsibility. Ask AI to list every commitment you made, every item the other person agreed to send, and every question that remains unanswered. Commitments you made Items the prospect agreed to provide Questions you need to answer Decisions that still belong to the prospect Statements that require confirmation This is where many follow-ups go wrong. The email sounds warm, but it forgets the document you said you would send or quietly assumes that the other person is ready to buy. A promise ledger gives you a simple review point before you send anything. 3. Turn the ledger into a small action plan Next, ask for actions, not themes. Each action should have one owner, one verb, and a suggested due date based only on the timing discussed in the call. If no timing was discussed, say “timing to confirm” rather than making one up. Action: Send the preparation checklist. Owner: Me. Timing: Before the next call. Action: Confirm the decision timeline. Owner: Prospect. Timing: Unknown. Action: Answer the question about the service process. Owner: Me. Timing: In the follow-up. Keep the immediate list to three to five actions. Put longer-term ideas in a separate section called “later possibilities.” This prevents a useful call from turning into a task pile that makes the next step less likely to happen. 4. Draft a personal follow-up, then edit it yourself Only after the first three passes should you ask for a follow-up draft. Give AI the specific points that need to appear: what you heard, what you are sending, what you need from the other person, and the proposed next step. Use a prompt like this: “Write a short follow-up email based only on the approved notes below. Open by reflecting the person's main priority in plain language. Include the two commitments I made, one question I need answered, and one clear next step. Do not add enthusiasm, claims, urgency, or information that is not in the notes. Keep it conversational.” Then edit the draft. Remove anything that sounds unlike you. Replace broad phrases with the person's actual words when they fit. Check every date, name, promise, and question against the transcript. AI can give you a strong first draft, but you are still responsible for the relationship and the accuracy of the message. Use a consistent record after every call The real benefit appears when each conversation ends in the same place. Save a short record with five sections: Purpose: Why the call happened. Priority: What the person most wants to solve. Evidence: Relevant facts they stated. Open loop: What needs confirmation. Next step: Who does what and when. You can store this record in the place where you already manage contacts and tasks. The tool matters less than the habit. If your notes live in one place, your task list in another, and your follow-up draft in a third, the process will still feel heavy. Set a review rule for yourself: no call is complete until the record has been checked, the follow-up has been edited, and the next action has an owner. That rule turns the transcript into part of your operating rhythm. Three checks before you trust the output First, compare the stated priorities with the transcript. Did AI capture what mattered, or did it give extra weight to a minor detail? Second, inspect every claim and commitment. If you cannot point to the source in the conversation, label it as a question or remove it. Third, read the email aloud. If you would not say it to the person, rewrite it. Also check your handling rules before using any transcript. A call may contain financial, health, household, or other private information. Use the least amount of information needed for the task, and follow the requirements that apply to your business. Make the workflow sound like you A transcript workflow should save time without flattening your voice. Keep a short instruction that describes how you communicate: whether you prefer brief emails, direct questions, warm openings, or clear choices. Add two examples of follow-ups you are proud to send, with private details removed. That reference gives AI a better target than a request to “sound professional.” It also gives you a repeatable way to spot when the draft has drifted. You can read more about checking whether an AI system sounds like you in the You-Replacement Test , and about follow-up writing in the three-pass email method . One good discovery call should produce clarity, not a second administrative job. Use AI for the sorting, labeling, and first draft. Keep the judgment, final edits, and human connection with you. When every call ends with a verified record and one clear next step, your business becomes easier to run one conversation at a time. If you want a larger set of practical workflows for creating authority and running your business, learn the AI system .

## FAQ

Q: What should I give AI besides the call transcript?
A: Give it the purpose of the call, your definition of a qualified opportunity, and any follow-up rules you already use. Do not add information that was not discussed or verified.

Q: Can AI decide whether I should take on a client?
A: AI can organize the evidence and point out open questions, but you should make the decision. Review the summary against the actual conversation before acting on it.

Q: How long should the final action list be?
A: Keep the immediate list short. Three to five actions for the next few days is usually easier to review and finish than a long list of every possible task.

Q: How do I keep an AI follow-up email from sounding generic?
A: Ask AI to use only details from the conversation, name the client's stated priority, and leave out broad promises. Then edit the draft until it sounds like something you would actually send.

Q: What if my transcript contains sensitive information?
A: Follow your professional and company rules before placing a transcript into an AI tool. Remove information you do not need for the task and check the tool's current privacy terms yourself.

# Past-Client AI Nurture: The 12-Month Touch System That Brings Referrals Back

URL: https://kristamashore.ai/articles/past-client-ai-nurture-12-month-touch-system
Pillar: Community Market Leaders®: AI for Real Estate & Lenders
Published: 2026-05-24T16:08:49.934Z
Author: Krista Mashore

Most agents drop their past clients within 90 days of closing. Here's the 12-month touch system that brings them back, AI-assisted where it should be.

You sold a couple a house in March of 2023. Beautiful closing, hugs in the driveway, you sent them a charcuterie board, and then you got busy with the next deal. It's now mid-2026. They just listed with someone else. You found out from Instagram. You felt sick about it for two days. This happens to good agents every month and it's almost always the same problem. You closed the deal, you moved on, and somebody else stayed in their inbox for three years while you didn't. The fix is a 12-month touch system. AI handles most of it. The two or three touches that matter most stay human. Below is the schedule I run with my coaching clients and the exact tools that make it actually possible. Why past clients matter more than cold leads The Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers has shown for years that a large share of sellers either use an agent they've worked with before or were referred by someone in their network. The most recent figures I've seen put repeat-and-referral business well over half of total transactions for established agents, with top agents often citing 70 to most their pipeline coming from past clients and the people those clients send. You should pull the current numbers directly from the official research page before quoting them publicly: see for the latest Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The point is this. Past clients are the highest-ROI asset you own. They already trust you. They've already paid you. They know how you work. And they're the cheapest, fastest source of the next deal, if you stay in front of them. The problem isn't that agents don't believe this. The problem is that staying in front of 200 past clients for 12 months is a lot of work and most agents quit by month three. AI changes that math. The 12-Month Touch Schedule Twelve touches over twelve months. Some are automated, some are AI-assisted, some are pure human. Here's the schedule. Month 1 (closing month). Closing gift drop. HUMAN. Don't outsource this. Walk it over yourself if they're local. Mail it with a handwritten card if they're not. AI cannot do this and it shouldn't. Month 2. "How's the house?" check-in text. HUMAN, AI-drafted. A real text from your phone. Have Claude draft it based on what you remember from the closing (kid's name, the dog, the kitchen remodel they were planning). Then rewrite it in your own thumbs. Send. Month 3. Market update email. AI. A short note. "Here's what's happening in your zip code since you bought." Automate this through your CRM. Tools like Follow Up Boss, kvCORE, or Sierra Interactive will pipe MLS data in. Have Claude write the human-sounding intro, not the canned market update template. Month 4. Home anniversary "did you know" tip. AI. A short email or video. Something useful. Filter changes for HVAC. The right time to fertilize. Permit reminders if they were planning a remodel. HeyGen with your own avatar makes the video version cheap to produce. Month 5. Phone call. HUMAN. Not a text. Not an email. Pick up the phone. AI is not allowed here. You're going to want to skip this one. Don't. This is the touch that creates referrals. Month 6. Six-month "how's the house feeling" survey. AI-handled, human-reviewed. A 3-question email. "What's working? What's not? What would you change?" Anything they flag gets a personal reply from you, not an autoresponder. The replies are gold for the next year of content. Month 7. Useful local content. AI-drafted, human-curated. A short roundup of what's opening in town, what's worth driving to, school district news, summer events. Local. Specific. Useful. AI drafts the structure, you add the one inside thing nobody else has. Month 8. Birthday or move-in anniversary card. HUMAN, with AI assist. Real card. Real handwriting. Use a service like Handwrytten or Postable if you must, but write the message yourself. AI helps you remember the date, not write the words. Month 9. Tax/financial reminder. AI. A short note about the home-related tax stuff (property tax due dates, homestead exemption if relevant, the IRS 1098 for mortgage interest if it's tax season). Useful. Not salesy. Month 10. "Who do you know?" referral ask. HUMAN, with AI script. The direct ask. Not "if you know anyone." Specific. "Hey, do you know anybody at your office who's been talking about moving?" Claude can draft three variations for you to pick from. The send button is yours. Month 11. Pop-by drop. HUMAN. If they're local, drop something off. Pumpkins in fall, fresh tomatoes in summer, holiday cookies in December. Cheap. Memorable. Almost nobody does this anymore so it lands hard. Month 12. Year-in-review note plus market temperature read. AI-drafted, you review. What happened in their zip code this year. Average sale price change. Days on market. Whether the inventory shifted. Their home is probably worth a different number than it was a year ago. Give them the read. What AI handles vs. what stays human The line is simpler than it sounds. AI handles anything repeatable, anything data-driven, and anything that scales. Humans handle anything that requires a heartbeat. AI handles: - Market update emails (the data layer) - Anniversary reminders firing into your calendar - Drafting the first version of every email and text - Filtering past-client replies and routing them to you - Producing the video version of any tip using your AI avatar Humans handle: - The closing gift - The Month 5 phone call - The handwritten card moments - The actual conversation when someone replies - Anything emotional, personal, or trust-building If you forget that line and let AI do the human touches, you'll feel the drop-off. Past clients can tell when they're being marketed to by a bot. The whole point of this system is that they don't feel marketed to at all. The stack I'd actually use in 2026 You can run this with a small stack. You don't need 14 tools. A CRM that holds your past-client list and fires off the scheduled emails. Follow Up Boss is what I see most coaching clients use. kvCORE and Sierra Interactive also work. Pick one and stick with it for two years. Claude with a Project for your brand voice. Every email, text, and script draft runs through it. Costs about $20 a month. If you've never set one up, my piece on claude-projects-setting-up-first-one walks through it. HeyGen for the video versions of your monthly tips. Saves the production cost. Don't overuse the AI avatar. One avatar video a month is fine. Five feels weird. Handwrytten for the card touches if your handwriting is illegible. Better than skipping the card. A simple spreadsheet or your CRM's task feature to track which touch each past client got. Even the best CRM lets people fall through if you don't audit monthly. That's it. Five tools. Maybe $80 a month total if you're already on a CRM. Why this works It works because past clients want to hear from you and almost nobody bothers. Twelve touches a year breaks down to one a month. One a month is sustainable. AI does the heavy drafting so you're not staring at a blinking cursor at 10pm. The human touches are the ones that prove you're still real. The agents in my Level Up program who run this system are pulling 60 to a lot of their annual transactions from past clients and referrals within 24 months of starting. That's not magic. That's the math of staying in front of 200 people for a year while everybody else forgets. Want the full schedule and templates? I built out every one of these 12 touches with the actual email templates, the phone call scripts, the Claude prompts, and the CRM setup steps inside Level Up. If you want the whole thing handed to you, come look at the program .

## FAQ

Q: How many past clients do I need before this is worth doing?
A: Even 20. The system works at any volume. If you have 20 past clients and one refers a deal this year, you've covered the cost of your whole stack for two years.

Q: What if I haven't talked to my past clients in years?
A: Start with a re-introduction email. It's been a while, here's what's been going on in your zip code since you bought, and I'd love to catch up. Then begin the 12-month schedule from there.

Q: Can AI write the phone call script for Month 5?
A: It can draft a script. Do not read it. Use it as a memory jog. The call has to feel like you, not a telemarketer.

Q: What CRM should I pick?
A: Whatever you'll actually use. I see Follow Up Boss most often with coaching clients, but kvCORE and Sierra Interactive both work. The CRM matters less than whether you log in.

Q: How do I keep AI from making everything sound the same?
A: Build a brand voice doc and load it into a Claude Project. Then every draft runs through your voice, not generic AI voice. Without this step, your past clients will feel the tone change immediately.

Q: Do I really need a video tip every month?
A: No. One a quarter is fine if monthly is too much. The 12-touch schedule is the floor, not the ceiling. Some months you'll have something better to send.
